Chapter 1 · Tutorial 1

Introduction to Pathology

Brief overview of cell and molecular biology

Pathology is the scientific study of disease. This chapter fixes the vocabulary and the three questions that every later chapter is really answering.

Know these cold

  • Disease = abnormal structure and/or function; disturbed homeostasis
  • Symptom (reported) vs sign (observed)
  • Aetiology → pathogenesis → morphologic & functional change
  • Cellular vs molecular pathology
  • Genetic vs environmental vs multifactorial causation

What disease is

Disease is a state of abnormal structure and/or abnormal function affecting cells, tissues, organs or systems — a condition in which normal homeostasis is disturbed, producing impaired physiological, biochemical or behavioural function. Homeostasis is the body's ability to keep its internal environment stable within a range; disease begins when that range is exceeded and not restored.

Tutorial 1 MCQs 1–3 are these three definitions verbatim. One clean sentence each.

A disease is a recognisable clinical entity built from three consistent elements:

SymptomsSubjective — what the patient experiences and reports: pain, fatigue, nausea, feeling unwell.
SignsObjective — what the clinician can observe or measure: swelling, fever, erythema, a lesion, a raised biomarker.
Pathological abnormalitiesThe underlying structural and functional change in the tissue itself.

How disease varies clinically

Every disease can be placed on three axes, and describing a case means placing it on all three:

AxisOne endOther end
Time courseAcute — rapid onset, short duration (appendicitis, herpetic gingivostomatitis)Chronic — slow onset, prolonged (periodontitis, rheumatoid arthritis)
ExtentLocalised — confined to one site (periapical abscess)Systemic — body-wide (SLE, sepsis)
OutcomeReversible — full recovery of structure and functionIrreversible — permanent loss (infarct, scar)

What pathology is

Pathology is the scientific study of disease. It explains what disease is, why it happens, and how it affects the body, connecting basic science → clinical signs and symptoms → investigations → diagnosis → treatment. It has two roles: a scientific discipline (understanding mechanisms — systematic observation, hypothesis-driven investigation, disease models) and a diagnostic discipline (interpreting samples from living patients to guide care).

Why it matters in clinical practice

Accurate diagnosisTurns symptoms and signs into a named entity; confirms or refines clinical impressions (benign vs malignant); avoids harmful misclassification.
Evidence-based treatmentTherapy targets mechanisms — infection, inflammation, thrombosis, malignancy — and can be stratified by severity, subtype, stage and risk, including "no treatment".
Prevention & public healthIdentifies causes and modifiable risks; enables screening and early detection; supplies registry and surveillance data.
Monitoring & prognosisBiomarkers and findings track response to treatment; grade, stage and molecular features predict outcome.
Tutorial 1 SAQ: "Explain why pathology is important in clinical practice" — these four rows are the answer.

The three core questions

Every disease is approached by asking, in order: aetiology (the cause), pathogenesis (the mechanism by which the cause produces disease), and the morphologic and functional changes that result. The morphologic and functional changes are what produce the signs and symptoms.

QuestionWhat it coversSmoking → lung cancer
1. AetiologyGenetic factors (inherited or acquired mutations); environmental factors (infection, toxins, radiation, nutrition); lifestyle and exposures (smoking, alcohol, occupation); immune and inflammatory triggers; multifactorial gene–environment interaction.Tobacco carcinogens acting on genetic susceptibility
2. PathogenesisMolecular and cellular pathways disrupted; the host response (inflammation, immunity, repair); progression over time — acute → chronic, reversible → irreversible.DNA adducts → mutations → disordered cell-cycle control → clonal proliferation
3. Morphologic + functional changeMorphology — gross and microscopic architecture. Function — organ performance, biomarkers, physiological consequences. Clinical correlation — symptoms, signs, complications, prognosis.Bronchial mass, dysplasia on histology; impaired gas exchange; cough, haemoptysis, weight loss

Structure and function

The core idea of the whole subject: disease = disturbed structure and disturbed function. Normal structure underpins normal function; structural change produces predictable functional impairment; and functional change may precede visible structural change. Pathology is the bridge that explains how anatomy becomes clinical disease.

Cellular pathology

The 19th-century introduction of light microscopy allowed thin tissue sections to be examined, revealed disease at the cellular level, overturned spontaneous generation and moved pathology from organ-level description to cellular analysis. Cells are the smallest functional units of life, and disease is explained by cell injury, adaptation and death — Virchow's omnis cellula e cellula. Two ideas carry forward: the same cellular components that keep a cell healthy become the sites of disease when they fail, and the products a cell secretes are altered in disease — both under- and over-production can be pathological.

Limits of cellular pathology

Some diseases show minimal structural change; functional disturbance may precede visible injury; biochemical and molecular defects can be primary. That is why molecular pathology exists — it reveals what a microscope cannot see.

Molecular pathology

Molecular pathology studies disease at the level of genes and proteins. The primary lesion may be molecular before any structural change is visible.

Initial faultConsequenceResult
DNA sequence change (SNV, insertion/deletion); chromosomal abnormalities (deletion, translocation, aneuploidy); epigenetic change (methylation, chromatin); altered gene expressionAbnormal proteins — wrong structure, folding, function or localisationDegenerative disease, toxic aggregates
Enzyme defects — metabolic blockToxic accumulation or deficiency (inborn errors)
Receptor / signalling defectsInappropriate growth and survival signalling
Disordered cell-cycle controlNeoplasia

Clinical impact: it explains congenital disease and cancer biology, and enables precision medicine — molecular profiling (subclassification beyond morphology; prognostic and predictive biomarkers) → targeted therapies (directed at specific pathways, avoiding ineffective treatment) → individualised, dynamically adjusted care. Precision medicine is impossible without modern pathology.

Cellular vs molecular — the comparison the tutorial asks for

Cellular pathologyMolecular pathology
LevelCell and tissue — what the microscope seesGenes and proteins — sequence, expression, signalling
Explains disease asCell injury, adaptation, death; altered architectureMutation, abnormal protein, enzyme or receptor defect, epigenetic change
TimingRequires visible structural changeLesion may be present before any structural change
StrengthFast, cheap, universal; basis of histopathological diagnosisExplains congenital disease and cancer biology; enables targeted therapy
LimitMisses functional/biochemical disease with normal morphologyNeeds clinical and morphological anchoring to be meaningful

Cellular and molecular injury — the targets

Whatever the cause, injury targets specific structures, and each target produces a predictable outcome. This table is the bridge into Chapter 2.

TargetWhat goes wrongOutcomes
NucleusDNA damage, mutations, impaired repair; viral integrationDysplasia → malignant transformation; cell death
MitochondriaReduced ATP, oxidative stress, release of pro-apoptotic factorsEnergy failure; apoptosis/necrosis; organ dysfunction
Membrane & transportIon channel and pump failure, permeability change, receptor/signalling failureCell swelling, oedema, impaired excitability
ProteinsMisfolding and accumulation, ER stress, impaired degradationDegenerative disease, toxic aggregates

Patterns of response: adaptation (hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, metaplasia) vs reversible injury vs irreversible injury (necrosis, apoptosis).

Where pathological knowledge comes from

Human patient material is the most important source: biopsies (incisional, excisional, needle), resections, cytology (exfoliative, aspirates), body fluids (blood, urine, CSF, pleural/peritoneal/synovial), autopsy tissue with clinicopathological correlation. Experimental systems support it: animal models, cell culture, organoids, computational models. The translational pathway runs bench discovery → validation in human samples → clinical implementation, and pathology must stay clinically anchored: findings matter because they change patient care. Diagnostic pathology also runs serial investigations — monitoring progression, response to treatment, recurrence.

What causes disease

Establishing the cause is the central question. Three categories: genetic, environmental, and multifactorial (gene–environment interaction), the last accounting for most common chronic disease.

Genetic causesEnvironmental causes
Inherited genetic abnormalities; prenatally acquired mutations; postnatally acquired genetic damage; monogenic vs polygenic; variable age of onset.Chemical (industrial/domestic chemicals, tobacco, alcohol, drugs); physical (mechanical trauma, temperature extremes, ionising and non-ionising radiation); infective (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, prions). Depend on dose, duration and exposure; carry potential for prevention.

Clues that separate genetic from environmental aetiology

Age of onset; pattern within families; stability vs reversibility; geographic and temporal distribution; response to removal of the exposure. Evidence comes from family aggregation, twin concordance (identical vs non-identical), adoption studies (separate shared genes from shared environment) and migrant populations.

Migrant study: a disease common in Japan, rare in the USA, and Japanese migrants acquire US rates within a generation → environmental. Genes travel with you; risk did not.

Predisposing factors and multifactorial disease

Predisposing factors and disease precursors: genetic susceptibility; host factors (immunity, nutrition, age); preneoplastic conditions; permissive diseases. Prenatal and early-life influences (transplacental toxins and infection, critical developmental windows, foetal nutrition) programme lifelong risk. Most common chronic diseases are multifactorial: multiple genetic variants plus environmental exposures, with threshold effects and variable clinical expression. The integrated framework's single principle: disease is the biological outcome of interacting influences, not a single event — and understanding causation guides diagnosis, identifies preventable factors, predicts behaviour and informs treatment and prognosis.

Drill

A patient reports pain and fatigue; on examination there is facial swelling and a temperature of 38.4 °C. Classify each finding, then frame the case with the three core questions.

Pain and fatigue are symptoms (subjective, reported). Swelling and fever are signs (objective, observed or measured). Aetiology: what caused it — e.g. a necrotic pulp with periapical infection. Pathogenesis: how — bacterial spread into bone and soft tissue producing acute inflammation and an abscess. Morphologic/functional change: pus-filled cavity, tissue destruction; pain, swelling, trismus.

Compare cellular and molecular pathology in three sentences.

Cellular pathology explains disease through what the microscope shows — cell injury, adaptation and death, and altered tissue architecture — and is the basis of histopathological diagnosis. Molecular pathology explains disease at the level of genes and proteins, where the primary lesion may exist before any structural change is visible. Cellular pathology tells you what has happened; molecular pathology tells you why, and enables targeted therapy.

Describe the relationship between structure and function in pathology.

Normal structure underpins normal function, so structural change produces predictable functional impairment (a fibrosed valve cannot open; an infarcted myocardium cannot contract). Functional change can precede visible structural change (a channelopathy, early enzyme defects), which is where molecular pathology takes over. Disease is defined as disturbance of both, and pathology is the bridge that explains how altered anatomy becomes clinical illness.

Chapter 2 · Tutorial 2

Cellular Responses to Stress & Injury

Adaptation, injury and the two routes to cell death

Cells sit in a steady state. Stress disturbs it, and the cell must adapt, recover, or die. Everything downstream in the course — inflammation, healing, neoplasia — begins with what happens to a single stressed cell.

Know these cold

  • Four adaptations: hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, metaplasia — apoptosis is not one
  • Labile / stable / permanent cells
  • Ischaemia removes O₂ and glucose → worse than hypoxia
  • Reversible injury: swelling, fatty change, nucleus intact. Irreversible: membrane failure, nucleus lost
  • Apoptosis vs necrosis — membrane intact vs ruptured decides everything

Injury and the response to injury

The lecture rests on one four-step chain: a stress is placed on cells and tissues → their structure and function change → they react to maintain homeostasis → the pathological process produces microscopic then macroscopic change, which manifests as signs and symptoms. There are only two destinations — adaptation (the cell survives) or cell death — and which one occurs depends on two variables: the properties of the injury (type, severity, duration) and the cells and tissues involved.

Homeostasis is the steady state in which cells are maintained, within a range. Stress and injury alter it. Cells may adapt or succumb; a cell may die from a sustained or progressive injurious stimulus even if it initially adapted.

Tutorial 2 SAQ 1: define homeostasis and what happens when disrupted → adaptation if possible; reversible then irreversible injury if not; death by necrosis or apoptosis.

Cell types by regenerative capacity

Whether a tissue can respond by dividing depends on its cells. This classification decides which adaptation is available now, and whether the tissue can regenerate in Chapter 5.

TypeDividing behaviourExamples
LabileDivide throughout life — continuously renewing, functionally short-lived; can increase their rate if requiredSurface epithelia (oral mucosa, skin), GI lining, bone marrow, lymphoid cells
StableDivide when needed — normally quiescent but recruited after injury; restore number and function though architecture may be abnormalLiver, kidney tubules, fibroblasts, smooth muscle
PermanentDivide only during foetal life — cannot replace themselves after birth; replaced by scar with loss of functionNeurons, cardiac and skeletal (striated) muscle

Injury to permanent cells — after an infarct or nerve damage — cannot be repaired by regeneration; it is replaced by scar with permanent loss of function. The liver regenerates after partial resection because it is stable; the heart scars after an infarct because it is permanent.

The four adaptations

Adaptation is usually a response to variations in functional demand. There are four, and whether a tissue can respond by hyperplasia depends on its cell type: permanent cells can only hypertrophy; labile and stable cells can also hyperplase.

Hypertrophy — increase in cell size

The organ enlarges because each cell grows — more organelles and proteins — not because there are more cells. The pure example is cardiac myocytes under pressure load (hypertension, aortic stenosis): heart cells are permanent and cannot divide, so they can only grow larger. Skeletal muscle with training is the physiological example.

Hyperplasia — increase in cell number

Physiologic: hormonal (breast in puberty and pregnancy, endometrium in the cycle) or compensatory (liver after resection). Pathologic: excess hormonal or growth-factor stimulation (endometrial hyperplasia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, gingival hyperplasia under drugs or plaque). The gravid uterus enlarges by both mechanisms — smooth muscle cells hypertrophy and hyperplase — which is why it is the lecture's set-piece comparison.

Tutorial 2 SAQ 2: hypertrophy = ↑ size (cardiac muscle in hypertension); hyperplasia = ↑ number (endometrium; gravid uterus does both).

Atrophy — decrease in size and/or number of cells

Physiologic atrophyPathologic atrophy
Development — normal remodelling (thymus, notochord, ductus arteriosus); ageingDecreased function / disuse (immobilised limb); denervation; loss of blood supply; pressure (tumour or cyst on adjacent tissue); lack of nutrition; loss of stimulation (endocrine, e.g. after menopause)

Mechanism: protein degradation (ubiquitin–proteasome, autophagy) exceeds synthesis, so the cell shrinks to a size at which survival is possible with reduced demand. Cells that shrink may eventually be lost.

Dental relevance — the residual ridge. After teeth are lost the alveolar bone is no longer loaded through the periodontal ligament. With loss of functional stimulation and altered pressure the residual ridge atrophies — a central consideration in denture design and implant planning.

Tutorial 2 scenario — muscle wasting after bed rest: disuse atrophy, pathologic (physiologic is limited to development and ageing). Reduced load → less protein synthesis, more degradation → fibres shrink. Reversible with reloading.

Metaplasia — change of cell type

Metaplasia is the transformation of one mature tissue type into another — usually reversible, and usually into a cell type better able to withstand a chronic stress. It arises by reprogramming of stem cells, not by transformation of mature cells. Examples: bronchial ciliated columnar → squamous in smokers (loses mucociliary clearance); Barrett's oesophagus — squamous → columnar (intestinal-type) under chronic acid reflux.

Barrett's oesophagus, worked. Contributing factors: chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux (obesity, hiatus hernia, alcohol, smoking, male sex). The metaplastic columnar epithelium tolerates acid better, so the change is adaptive — but the influences that drive metaplasia can, if persistent, drive dysplasia and then adenocarcinoma. Implications: increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, therefore endoscopic surveillance, acid suppression and lifestyle change. Adaptation is not always benign.

Causes of cell injury

When adaptation is not possible, injury results. Four categories from the lecture: physicochemical agents (trauma, temperature, radiation, chemicals, toxins); biological agents (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites); loss of stimulation (withdrawal of hormonal or growth-factor signals); deprivation (oxygen and glucose). Add immune reactions (Chapter 6), genetic defects and nutritional imbalance for a complete list.

Targets

Whatever the cause, injurious stimuli affect three targets: cell and organelle membranes, metabolic pathways (ATP generation in mitochondria), and DNA and proteins. Cellular processes are inter-dependent, so an insult to one organelle deranges another — injury cascades.

Tutorial 2 MCQ 4 — ischaemia primarily affects: d) cell and organelle membranes and metabolic pathways.

Ischaemia and hypoxia

TermMeaningExample
IschaemiaReduced blood supply — both oxygen and glucose fall, and metabolites are not removedAtherosclerosis, thrombus, embolus
HypoxiaReduced oxygen supply specifically, with flow maintainedPneumonia, anaemia, CO poisoning

Sequence: ↓ O₂ → ↓ oxidative phosphorylation → ↓ ATP → Na⁺/K⁺ pump fails (cell swelling, ER dilation, blebs), anaerobic glycolysis (↓ pH, glycogen depleted), ribosomes detach (↓ protein synthesis) → if prolonged, mitochondrial and lysosomal membrane damage, Ca²⁺ influx activating phospholipases and proteases → membrane rupture → necrosis. Ischaemia is more damaging than hypoxia alone because it starves the cell of both its fuel and the oxygen needed to burn it, and the anaerobic pathway that rescues a hypoxic cell is also cut off.

Ionising radiation

Radiation that forms ions on interaction with matter. Electromagnetic: X-rays, gamma rays. Particulate: alpha (helium nuclei), beta (electrons), neutrons. Acts mainly indirectly through reactive oxygen species and also directly on DNA and proteins.

Deterministic effectsStochastic effects
Severity rises with dose; there is a threshold below which they do not occur — skin burns, mucositis, cataractOnly the probability rises with dose, not the severity; no safe threshold — radiation-induced cancer, heritable mutation

Rapidly dividing tissues are most sensitive. The radiographer's scatter dose is a stochastic concern: one ionising event can in principle produce a mutation, so risk falls with dose but never reaches zero.

Reversible vs irreversible injury

The single most important distinction in cell injury: can the cell still recover? If the stimulus persists or is severe, the cell crosses a threshold, becomes irreversibly injured and dies. The two hallmarks of irreversibility are inability to restore mitochondrial function and profound membrane disturbance.

Reversible injuryIrreversible injury
Hydropic degeneration (cellular swelling) — pump failure lets Na⁺ and water in; cytoplasm pale/vacuolated, more eosinophilic; ER dilated; membrane blebs; mitochondrial swelling. Fatty change — lipid vacuoles from dissociation of lipid from protein (liver, heart). Nucleus intact.Membrane rupture and lysosomal enzyme leak; mitochondrial amorphous densities; nuclear change — pyknosis (shrunken, dense), karyorrhexis (fragmented), karyolysis (dissolved). Loss of the nucleus is the key marker.

The lecture's histology contrasts normal kidney tubules with reversibly injured tubules (swollen and vacuolated but architecturally intact) and irreversibly injured tubules (loss of nuclei and architecture).

Tutorial 2 SAQ 3: reversible vs irreversible + microscopic changes of reversible injury → cellular swelling and fatty change, nucleus preserved.

Cell death

Necrosis

Unintended, pathologic cell death following irreversible injury. Cell contents leak out, which elicits inflammation in the surrounding tissue. Patterns worth knowing: coagulative (ischaemia in solid organs — architecture preserved, cells eosinophilic and anucleate), liquefactive (brain; bacterial infection → pus), caseous (TB — "cheesy"), fat necrosis, fibrinoid (immune complexes in vessel walls), gangrenous (limb ischaemia ± infection).

Autophagy

The cell digests its own organelles and uses the products as nutrients — a survival strategy under stress such as starvation, a last-ditch attempt at homeostasis. If the cell can no longer cope, autophagy gives way to apoptosis.

Apoptosis

Programmed cell death, which may be physiologic or pathologic. The cell fragments in a controlled way, there is no inflammatory response, and harmful lysosomal contents are contained. Physiologic: embryogenesis, hormone-dependent involution, deletion of self-reactive lymphocytes, removal of neutrophils at the end of acute inflammation. Pathologic: DNA damage, misfolded proteins, viral infection, cytotoxic T-cell killing.

Inhibitors (promote survival)Inducers (trigger death)
Growth factors; extracellular matrix attachment; sex steroids; some viral proteinsGrowth-factor withdrawal; loss of matrix attachment; glucocorticoids; some viruses; free radicals; ionising radiation; DNA damage; ligand binding at death receptors (Fas, TNF)

Two pathways converge on caspases: the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway — the balance of anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 / Bcl-xL against pro-apoptotic Bak / Bax decides whether cytochrome c leaks from mitochondria; and the extrinsic (death-receptor) pathway. p53 senses DNA damage, attempts repair, and triggers apoptosis if repair fails. Loss of p53 — the commonest mutation in cancer — lets DNA-damaged cells survive and accumulate further mutations.

Apoptosis vs necrosis

FeatureApoptosisNecrosis
NatureProgrammed, regulated, active (needs ATP)Unintended, unregulated; occurs with energy failure
TriggerPhysiologic or pathologicAlways pathologic — severe injury
Cell sizeShrinks and fragmentsSwells and ruptures
MembraneIntact; contents packaged into apoptotic bodiesLost; contents leak out
NucleusChromatin condenses, fragments neatlyPyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis
InflammationNone — phagocytosed silentlyYes — leaked contents provoke it
ScaleSingle cellsGroups of cells, tissue

Apoptosis is tidy, deliberate and silent; necrosis is messy, accidental and inflammatory. Every other difference follows from whether the membrane stays intact.

DNA damage and radiotherapy

A DNA-damaged cell has three fates: death (immediately or at the next mitosis), repair (no consequence), or permanent change in genotype — the basis of neoplasia. Radiotherapy induces DNA damage in tumour cells and works because cancer cells divide rapidly; but normal rapidly dividing cells — oral mucosa, bone marrow, hair follicles — are equally sensitive. Oral mucosa is labile and therefore among the most radiosensitive normal tissues, which is why mucositis is the reliable complication of head-and-neck radiotherapy.

Drill

Why does necrosis cause inflammation but apoptosis does not?

In necrosis the membrane fails and lysosomal enzymes and cytoplasmic contents leak into the interstitium; those leaked contents are the mediators that provoke an inflammatory response. In apoptosis the membrane stays intact and the cell packages itself into apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed by macrophages with no leak — so nothing triggers inflammation.

A hypertensive patient has an enlarged heart; a pregnant patient has an enlarged uterus. Same mechanism?

No. Cardiac myocytes are permanent cells and can only enlarge — pure hypertrophy. Uterine smooth muscle is stable and enlarges by both hypertrophy and hyperplasia under oestrogen. The cell type decides which adaptation is available.

Give three causes of cell injury with an example of each, and name the three cellular targets.

Deprivation — ischaemia from coronary atherosclerosis. Physicochemical — ionising radiation causing mucositis. Biological — viral infection of hepatocytes. (Also loss of stimulation, immune reactions, genetic defects.) Targets: membranes, metabolic pathways/ATP, and DNA/proteins.

A radiographer worries about small scatter doses. Which type of effect is the concern and why is there no safe dose?

Stochastic — radiation-induced cancer. Only the probability, not the severity, relates to dose; a single ionising event can produce a mutation, so risk falls with dose but never reaches zero. Deterministic effects (burns, mucositis) have a threshold below which they do not occur.

c) Apoptosis (it is cell death).
MCQ — atrophy
c) Decrease in cell size and/or number.

c) Labile cells.
MCQ — ischaemia primarily affects

SAQ — homeostasis and its disruption
Steady state within a range; stress alters it → adapt (hypertrophy/hyperplasia/atrophy/metaplasia) or injury → reversible → irreversible → death (necrosis/apoptosis).
SAQ — hypertrophy vs hyperplasia
Size vs number; cardiac muscle in hypertension vs endometrial hyperplasia; gravid uterus does both; permanent cells can only hypertrophy.
SAQ — reversible vs irreversible
Reversible: swelling (hydropic change), fatty change, ER dilation, blebs, nucleus intact. Irreversible: membrane rupture, mitochondrial densities, pyknosis/karyorrhexis/karyolysis → necrosis.
SAQ — causes of injury (3+)
Hypoxia/ischaemia, physical (trauma, radiation, temperature), chemical/toxins, biological agents, immune reactions, genetic, nutritional, loss of stimulation.
Scenario — bed-rest muscle atrophy
Disuse atrophy; pathologic. ↓ load → ↓ synthesis, ↑ degradation (ubiquitin–proteasome, autophagy) → fibre shrinkage ± loss; reversible with rehabilitation.
Scenario — Barrett's oesophagus
Metaplasia squamous → columnar from chronic reflux (obesity, hiatus hernia, alcohol, smoking). Adaptive but ↑ risk of dysplasia → adenocarcinoma; needs surveillance and acid suppression.
3

Chapter 3 · Tutorial 3

Acute Inflammation

The vascular and cellular response to injury, and its four outcomes

Inflammation is the connective tissue's response to injury — a reaction of blood vessels with accumulation of fluid and leukocytes. It exists to rid the body of the cause of injury and its consequences, and it hands over directly to repair.

Know these cold

  • Five cardinal signs and the mechanism behind each
  • Exudate (high protein, altered permeability) vs transudate (low protein, hydrostatic)
  • Three tissue events: flow/calibre → permeability → leukocyte emigration (M-A-D-C-P)
  • Immediate transient (endothelial gaps) vs immediate sustained (direct injury)
  • Four outcomes: resolution, suppuration, organisation/repair, chronicity

Vocabulary

ParenchymaThe functional part of an organ (a neuron, a hepatocyte). Parenchymal cells can sometimes regenerate.
StromaThe supporting connective tissue framework. Stroma repairs by laying down collagen. Parenchyma vs stroma is the distinction all of repair rests on.
Dystrophic calcificationMineralisation of soft tissue without a systemic mineral imbalance — calcium deposits in damaged or dying tissue, blood calcium normal.
CaseousCheesy in appearance — the necrosis of tuberculosis.
EndotheliumThe single flat cell layer lining blood and lymph vessels — the surface on which every vascular event below happens.
InfarctAn area of dead tissue caused by loss of blood supply.
-itisAdded to a tissue or organ name to denote inflammation of it — pulpitis, gingivitis, pericarditis, pancreatitis.
Pyo- / dia- / hyper- / cyto-Pus / through / excessive / cell — pyogenic = pus-producing; diapedesis = moving through a vessel wall.

Why inflammation exists, and what it is

An injurious stimulus damages parenchymal or stromal cells; the same stimulus provokes a complex reaction in the surrounding connective tissue. That reaction is inflammation. To resolve an injury the body must destroy, dilute or isolate the injurious agent and heal or replace the damaged tissue. Inflammation and repair are two halves of one process. Where inflammation is defective, infections never heal and wounds become permanent festering sores — inflammation is unpleasant, but its absence is far worse.

Inflammation is the connective tissue response to injury: a reaction of the blood vessels, with accumulation of fluid and leukocytes in the tissues. It is a protective response, but it can be harmful. Three properties: it is stereotyped (fundamentally the same regardless of tissue and cause), overlapping (a group of inter-related responses, not a tidy sequence) and shared with immunity (immune cells and inflammatory cells are the same cells — the bridge into Chapter 4).

Tutorial 3 SAQ 1: definition + purpose. Quote the definition, then "destroy, dilute or isolate the agent; heal or replace the tissue".

The inflammatory cells

Leukocytes (~7 million per mL of blood, two-thirds neutrophils, produced in bone marrow) defend against pathogens, identify and destroy foreign or abnormal cells, and clean up debris. They are highly mobile and travel to the injury.

CellRole
NeutrophilsPolymorphonuclear granulocytes. Phagocytic specialists, first-line defenders; two-thirds of circulating leukocytes; short-lived (die by apoptosis in 1–2 days). Neutrophil = acute.
EosinophilsAllergic conditions and defence against parasites (worms); stain red.
BasophilsLeast common; similar to mast cells — store histamine and heparin.
Monocytes / macrophagesMononuclear precursor phagocytes; in tissue they enlarge into macrophages that live months to years (the amount digested determines lifespan). Arrive ~48 h. Macrophage and lymphocyte = chronic.
LymphocytesB cells produce antibody and prime antigens for destruction; T cells mediate cellular immunity against cancer cells and virus-infected cells.

Which cell dominates a section is how a pathologist dates inflammation. A dense neutrophil infiltrate is minutes-to-days old; months old would show macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells and fibroblasts laying collagen.

Exudate, transudate, oedema, pus

TermDefinitionExample
ExudateInflammatory extravascular fluid with a high protein content; requires a significant alteration in vessel permeability. Contains fibrinogen (→ fibrin), immunoglobulins, complement, cells.Any inflammation — peritonitis, periapical abscess, pleurisy
TransudateLow-protein ultrafiltrate of plasma, from hydrostatic (or osmotic) imbalance across an endothelium of normal permeability.Left-sided cardiac failure (pulmonary oedema); hypoalbuminaemia (ascites); venous obstruction
OedemaExcess fluid in the interstitial spaces — can be either exudate or transudate.Either mechanism
PusA purulent exudate — rich in leukocytes (mainly neutrophils) and cellular debris, with dead and living bacteria.Abscess

Starling's law. Normally the osmotic (oncotic) pressure of plasma proteins almost exactly balances the hydrostatic pressure forcing fluid out. When hydrostatic pressure substantially exceeds osmotic pressure the balance tips and fluid accumulates — pulmonary oedema in left-sided heart failure. Other named exudates: serous (thin, protein-poor cellular fluid — blister), fibrinous (fibrin-rich, severe leak — pericarditis), haemorrhagic.

Tutorial 3 MCQ 3: exudate rich in leukocytes and debris = pus. SAQ 3: exudate vs transudate — the discriminator is protein, which reflects whether permeability changed.

Acute vs chronic

AcuteChronic
OnsetImmediate response to injuryDelayed
DurationMinutes to a maximum of ~2 daysWeeks to months
Dominant cellsNeutrophilsLymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages

There is temporal and cellular overlap — they are two ends of one continuum. A chronic lesion can have an acute exacerbation; an acute process can slide into chronicity.

Starting and stopping

Switching on: chemical mediators — singly, in combination, or in sequence — stimulate and amplify the response; sources include necrotic cells and mast cells. Switching off: when the injurious agent is removed and the mediators are displaced or inhibited. Read the stop condition carefully: if the body cannot remove or destroy the stimulus, the process cannot switch off — which is the definition of chronic inflammation.

The five cardinal signs

SignMeaningUnderlying change
RuborRednessArteriolar vasodilation and opening of capillary beds → hyperaemia
CalorHeatThe same increased blood flow bringing warm core blood to the surface
TumorSwellingIncreased vascular permeability → protein-rich exudate in the interstitium
DolorPainProstaglandins and bradykinin sensitise nerve endings; pressure of exudate
Functio laesaLoss of functionCombined effect of pain, swelling and tissue damage — the one most often forgotten
The four Latin signs all end in -or. Numbness is not a cardinal sign (Tutorial 3 MCQ 2).

What acute inflammation achieves

Three functional products, each mapping onto a goal: exudate — increased extracellular fluid that dilutes and flushes toxins (and delivers antibody, complement and fibrin); infiltrate — neutrophils and macrophages that destroy the agent; granulation tissue — the scaffolding for healing. Three tissue events deliver them.

Tissue event A — vascular flow and calibre

  1. Transient arteriolar vasoconstrictionseconds to minutes, easily overlooked, but the first event.
  2. Vasodilationarterioles first, then vessels that would otherwise be closed; new capillary beds open and flow increases → calor and rubor.
  3. Slowing of the circulation — stasisincreased permeability lets plasma out, red-cell concentration rises, blood becomes viscous and slows. Timing: 15–30 min with a mild stimulus, within minutes after severe injury.

Stasis has to happen before leukocytes can leave: in normal flow cells ride the fast axial stream; slowing and concentrating the blood lets white cells drift to the margins (margination). Without stasis they would be swept past the injury.

Tissue event B — vascular permeability

Occurs in the microcirculation. Normally interstitial fluid and plasma are in balance; during inflammation the endothelium becomes leaky and fluid containing proteins and cells leaves — an exudate — producing oedema.

MechanismFeatures
Endothelial gapsMost common. Histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes contract endothelial cells → intercellular gaps in post-capillary venules. Reversible and short-lived — the immediate transient response.
Cytoskeletal reorganisationCytokine-induced (IL-1, TNF); slower onset, reversible leakage.
Direct endothelial injuryNecrotising injuries (burns, lytic bacteria): endothelial necrosis and detachment. Immediate and sustained — lasts several hours.
Leukocyte-dependent injuryActivated leukocytes adhering to endothelium release enzymes and oxygen species and damage the vessel.
Leakage from new vesselsDuring repair — immature vessels are inherently leaky.

Classic experiment: carbon particles injected into a rat followed by histamine labelled the leak sites precisely — the post-capillary venules. Endothelium becomes leaky either from direct injury or via chemical mediators.

Tutorial 3 MCQ 4: immediate transient leakage is caused by endothelial gaps. Examiners pair "immediate transient" against "immediate sustained" (direct injury).

Tissue event C — leukocyte emigration

Accumulation of leukocytes is the major feature of inflammation. Their job at the site is to engulf and degrade bacteria, immune complexes and debris. A defined sequence produces it:

  1. Margination (pavementing)during stasis white cells move from the axial stream to the vessel wall; pavementing is when the wall appears carpeted with them.
  2. Adhesionattachment to endothelium, blood flowing past without disturbing them. Rolling on selectins, then firm adhesion via integrins binding ICAM-1 / VCAM-1 that cytokines have up-regulated on the endothelium.
  3. Diapedesisthe white cell moves through the vessel wall (between endothelial cells, then across the basement membrane) into interstitial fluid by amoeboid movement.
  4. Chemotaxisunidirectional migration along a chemical gradient (C5a, LTB4, chemokines, bacterial products). Directed, not random.
  5. Phagocytosis and intracellular degradation.
  6. Extracellular release of leukocyte productswhich can damage the host.
M-A-D-C-P: reach the wall before you can stick, stick before you can cross, cross before you can follow a gradient. Diapedesis = getting out; chemotaxis = knowing where to go.

Phagocytosis — and how it harms the host

Phagocytosis is the ingestion and digestion of cell debris and micro-organisms. Four steps: recognition (aided by opsonins — IgG, C3b), adhesion, engulfment into a phagosome, killing/degradation when the phagosome fuses with a lysosome (phagolysosome; respiratory burst via NADPH oxidase, myeloperoxidase, lysosomal enzymes).

Failure modeWhat happens
Regurgitation during feedingThe phagocytic vacuole is not completely closed, so lysosomal contents spill into the tissue while the cell is still ingesting.
Frustrated phagocytosisThe cell attempts to digest non-digestible material — a flat surface, a suture, an implant, a urate crystal — cannot close a vacuole, and discharges its enzymes externally.

Both cause tissue damage, which further stimulates inflammation — a self-amplifying loop, and one important way a protective response becomes harmful. A retained suture provoking ongoing inflammation is frustrated phagocytosis with a stimulus that can never be removed — chronic inflammation de novo.

Chemical mediators — learn them by effect

EffectMediators
VasodilationProstaglandins (PGE₂, PGI₂), histamine, nitric oxide
Increased permeabilityHistamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes (C4, D4, E4), C3a/C5a
Chemotaxis and leukocyte activationComplement C5a, leukotriene B4, chemokines (IL-8), bacterial products
FeverProstaglandins (via IL-1, TNF)
PainProstaglandins, bradykinin
Tissue damageNeutrophil and macrophage contents — lysosomal enzymes, reactive oxygen species, NO

Prostaglandins account for vasodilation, fever and pain — which is why NSAIDs (cyclo-oxygenase inhibitors) are anti-inflammatory, antipyretic and analgesic at once. Histamine from mast cells is the first-minute mediator; complement is the amplifier shared with hypersensitivity.

Sequelae — the four outcomes

OutcomeWhat it needs / what it means
ResolutionComplete restoration of normal structure and function. Rare — requires a minor injury and labile (regenerating) cells with an intact stromal framework.
SuppurationPus formation (neutrophils, debris, pyogenic bacteria). An abscess is a localised collection of pus walled off by granulation tissue. Release of pus allows organisation and healing with scarring.
Organisation / repairThe most common outcome: granulation tissue → collagen → scar. Function not fully restored.
Progression to chronic inflammationWhen the agent cannot be removed — Chapter 4.

The abscess, worked (Tutorial 3 scenario)

Pyogenic bacteria (staphylococci) enter tissue → acute inflammation with intense neutrophil emigration → bacteria and neutrophils die; lysosomal enzymes liquefy the tissue → a cavity of pus (liquefactive necrosis) surrounded by a wall of fibrin, inflammatory cells and then granulation tissue (the pyogenic membrane). This is suppuration as an outcome of acute inflammation. Because it is walled off and its centre has no blood supply, neither immune cells nor antibiotics reach the pus reliably — incision and drainage is the definitive treatment. Untreated: expansion and pressure; spread through tissue planes (cellulitis, fascial-space infection — Ludwig's angina in the floor of the mouth); sinus or fistula formation as it tracks to a surface; bacteraemia, septicaemia, metastatic abscess; chronic abscess with fibrous wall; osteomyelitis if bone is involved.

Regeneration and repair

Two different words. Regeneration — replacement by parenchymal cell division; the functional tissue itself is restored. Repair — restoration by connective tissue; the defect is filled with collagen and function is not fully restored. Both replace tissue lost to necrosis.

  1. Neutralise the injurious agentthe cause must be dealt with first.
  2. Parenchymal cells regenerate / stromal cells repair.
  3. Neutralisation or decay of mediators.
  4. Return to normal vascular permeabilityexudation stops.
  5. Cessation of leukocyte infiltration.
  6. Death of neutrophils by apoptosisnot necrosis, so they are cleared without restarting inflammation (Chapter 2).
  7. Removal of waste by lymphatics.

Regeneration requires cells capable of division and differentiation and retention of the stroma — the architectural framework must survive or there is nothing to build on. Stem cells: undifferentiated, rapidly dividing; pluripotential (any cell type) or multipotential (a limited set, e.g. fibroblast → osteoblast). Repair (organisation) proceeds in three stages: granulation tissue (capillary budding + inflammatory exudate) → replacement by collagen (fibroblasts) → maturation into scar.

Dental relevance. Oral mucosa is labile, so minor mucosal injuries heal quickly and completely. A lingual or inferior alveolar nerve injury after third-molar surgery involves permanent cells — function may not return.

Wound types

A wound is any disruption of tissues or organs caused by injury, most commonly physical or mechanical trauma. Read the table as a spectrum of healing potential — everything in wound management tries to move a wound toward the surgical-incision end.

WoundFeaturesExample
AbrasionOpen, superficial — surface epithelium only; friction injuryCarpet burn
ContusionBruise — blunt injury damaging deep tissue with haemorrhage; surface intact, so no route for contaminationBlunt trauma
AvulsionLarge open wound with extensive loss of tissue volume — cutting, gouging, tearingAvulsion of a tooth from its socket
PunctureSmall, deep wound from a sharp object; contamination carried deepNeedle-stick; dog bite
LacerationOpen wound with ragged edges extending deep; crushed tissue, necrotic debris, clot; contaminatedLaceration of the tongue
Incisional / surgicalClean, aseptic; minimal tissue loss; sharp margins that can be approximated — ideal conditionsSurgical incision

The deep laceration, worked (Tutorial 3 scenario)

A deep laceration has crushed, contaminated edges and tissue loss, so it heals by second intention (Chapter 5): haemostasis and clot → acute inflammation (neutrophils, then macrophages debride necrotic tissue and bacteria) → granulation tissue (angiogenesis by endothelial cells, fibroblasts laying matrix) fills the defect → epithelial regeneration from labile keratinocytes at the margins → myofibroblast contraction → collagen remodelling into scar. Cells: neutrophils, macrophages, endothelial cells, fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, keratinocytes; skeletal muscle in the wound has only limited regeneration (satellite cells) and nerve regrows only if its sheath survives. Resolution vs scarring depends on: extent of tissue loss and whether the stroma survived; cell type; infection and foreign material; blood supply; approximation of edges (suturing moves it toward first intention); host factors — age, nutrition, diabetes, steroids, smoking.

Drill

List the five cardinal signs with meaning and one mechanism each.

Rubor (redness) — vasodilation. Calor (heat) — increased blood flow. Tumor (swelling) — exudate in the interstitium from increased permeability. Dolor (pain) — prostaglandins and bradykinin plus pressure of exudate. Functio laesa (loss of function) — the combined effect of pain, swelling and damage.

A pleural fluid sample has a low protein content. Is this inflammatory? Likely mechanism?

No — low protein makes it a transudate. Vessel permeability is normal; the fluid is a plasma ultrafiltrate driven by hydrostatic imbalance, classically cardiac failure. An inflammatory effusion would be a high-protein exudate because permeability itself is altered.

Name the five mechanisms of vascular leakage and the most common.

Endothelial gaps (most common; immediate transient), cytoskeletal reorganisation (cytokine-induced), direct injury (immediate sustained, several hours), leukocyte-dependent injury, leakage from new vessels during repair.

Why is complete resolution rare?

It requires a minor injury and a tissue of labile cells with its stroma intact. Most injuries are too extensive, destroy the framework, or occur in tissues whose cells cannot divide, so the defect is filled with connective tissue — repair with scarring.

Which single mediator class explains vasodilation, fever and pain, and what drug class targets it?

Prostaglandins; NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase and are therefore anti-inflammatory, antipyretic and analgesic through one mechanism.

Tutorial 3 — answer key

MCQ — suffix -itis
c) Inflammation.
MCQ — NOT a cardinal sign
d) Numbness.
MCQ — exudate rich in leukocytes and debris
b) Pus.
MCQ — immediate transient leakage
d) Endothelial gaps.
SAQ — define inflammation and its purpose
Connective tissue response to injury: vascular reaction with fluid and leukocyte accumulation. Purpose: destroy/dilute/isolate the agent, heal/replace tissue; protective but potentially harmful.
SAQ — five cardinal signs + mechanism
Rubor/calor — vasodilation and hyperaemia; tumor — exudate from ↑ permeability; dolor — prostaglandins, bradykinin, pressure; functio laesa — combined.
SAQ — exudate vs transudate
High protein, altered permeability, inflammation (abscess, peritonitis) vs low protein, hydrostatic imbalance, normal permeability (left heart failure, hypoalbuminaemia).
Scenario — abscess
Pyogenic bacteria → neutrophil emigration → liquefaction → pus walled by granulation tissue = suppuration. Complications: spread/cellulitis, sinus/fistula, bacteraemia/sepsis, chronicity, osteomyelitis. Needs drainage.
Scenario — deep laceration
Second-intention repair: clot → inflammation → granulation tissue → epithelialisation → contraction → scar. Cells: neutrophils, macrophages, endothelium, fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, keratinocytes. Outcome set by tissue loss, stroma, cell type, infection, foreign body, perfusion, approximation, host factors.

Chapter 4 · Tutorial 3B

Chronic Inflammation

The immune system that drives it, the forms it takes, and periodontal disease as the model

When the body cannot remove the injurious agent, inflammation cannot switch off. This chapter builds the immune system — antibodies, MHC, T and B cells, the macrophage — then uses it to explain granulomas, abscess tracts, ulcers, and why periodontitis never resolves on its own.

Know these cold

  • Chronic = prolonged (weeks–months), damage continues while healing is attempted
  • Cells: macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells (+ fibroblasts). Not neutrophils
  • CD4 ↔ MHC II (APCs); CD8 ↔ MHC I (any nucleated cell). 4×2 = 8, 8×1 = 8
  • Heavy chain sets Ig class; Fc region recruits cells and complement
  • Granuloma ≠ granulation tissue; Langhans' (horseshoe) vs foreign-body (scattered) giant cells
  • Plaque sits outside the body — the stop condition is never met

Immunity and inflammation

Immunity is a state of having sufficient biological defences to avoid infection, disease or other unwanted biological invasion. Two types with considerable overlap: specific (memory; targeted at a threat encountered before; humoral and cellular) and non-specific (inflammation — the cytokine-mediated response to an injurious stimulus; no memory). An immune response can trigger an inflammatory response, which is exactly what happens in chronic inflammatory disease.

Why memory changes everything. A bacterium inhaled for the first time damages the lung — both immune and inflammatory responses fire. Inhaled again with memory in place, it is destroyed by the specific response before much inflammation is needed, so there is little damage. That is the rationale for vaccination: install memory so the specific response acts before the destructive non-specific one is required. Immunity is double-edged: none (HIV, immunosuppression) → prey to simple infections and tumours; hyperactive → fatal immune-mediated disease (anaphylaxis after a bee sting).

Two arms: cell-mediated (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, macrophages; T cells and NK cells) and humoral (B cells and antibody).

Antigens and antibodies

Antigen: any substance the body regards as foreign or potentially dangerous — usually protein; in autoimmune disease the body recognises autoantigens, its own molecules, as foreign. Antibody: a blood protein synthesised in lymphoid tissue by plasma cells (activated B lymphocytes) in response to antigen; circulates to bind antigen and render it harmless; made of immunoglobulin, classified by structure and function.

Structure: two heavy and two light chains; the variable Fab arms bind antigen; the constant Fc stem binds cell receptors. The heavy chain determines the class (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE); the Fc region binds cell receptors and causes opsonisation, complement-mediated lysis and mast-cell degranulation.

ClassFunctionHook
IgAMucosal surfaces — the antibody of secretions; dominant immunoglobulin in saliva, first antibody defence at every oral mucosal surfacemucosAl
IgDAntigen receptor on B cellsB-cell Doorbell
IgEBinds allergens; triggers histamine release from mast cellsE-llergy
IgGThe majority of antibody-based immunity; crosses placenta; memoryGeneral workhorse
IgMThe early antibody, high avidity, secreted before there is enough IgGiMmediate
Raised IgM, low IgG against an organism = recent first exposure. IgG alone = established or past immunity.

MHC — the signpost system

The Major Histocompatibility Complex is a membrane protein complex all self cells display; three classes (I, II, III — III is complement, see Chapter 7). MHC proteins are signposts that display fragments of antigen — self or non-self — on the cell surface. A neutrophil or macrophage acquires non-self antigen by engulfment; an infected or cancerous cell displays abnormal antigen with class I. Viruses and cancer cells tend to display unusual non-self antigens, and those initiate specific immunity.

ClassFound onPresents to
MHC IAll nucleated cellsCD8+ cytotoxic T cells — any infected cell can be inspected and killed
MHC IIAntigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells)CD4+ helper T cells — whose job is to direct, not kill

T lymphocytes

Each T cell is genetically programmed to recognise one specific antigen via its T-cell receptor, and can only be activated by a surface-presented antigen — never a soluble one. Two types by co-receptor.

CD4+ helper T cellCD8+ cytotoxic T cell
The master regulator of the immune system. When activated it secretes cytokines (IL-2, IFN-γ, IL-4/5/13, IL-17) that influence every other immune cell — other T cells, B cells, macrophages, NK cells. Binds MHC II. HIV selectively destroys these cells; the symptoms of HIV show their importance. Subsets: Th1 (IFN-γ → macrophages), Th2 (IL-4/5/13 → IgE, eosinophils), Th17 (IL-17 → neutrophils).Primarily cytotoxic; can also secrete cytokines. Releases perforin and granulysin/granzymes that form pores in the target membrane — ions and water rush in, the cell swells and lyses (the necrosis pattern) — or induces apoptosis via Fas (the tidy pattern). Binds MHC I. Kills virus-infected and tumour cells.
Tutorial 3B MCQ 3: key mediator released by activated CD4+ cells = cytokines. Perforin and granulysin belong to CD8+.

Natural killer cells

A lymphocyte (large granular lymphocyte) with no T-cell receptor and no surface immunoglobulin. Lyses tumour cells, virally infected cells and some normal cells without previous sensitisation; has an Fc receptor for IgG so can kill IgG-coated cells (ADCC). Class I MHC protects normal cells from NK killing — so a virus-infected or cancer cell that evades CD8 cells by shedding MHC I becomes an NK target. Losing the identity badge is itself the trigger.

B lymphocytes and plasma cells

10–20% circulate; the rest reside in bone marrow, lymph nodes, spleen and tonsils. Each B cell carries a surface antigen receptor (IgM/IgD) of unique specificity. B cells can be activated by soluble antigen — unlike T cells — with help from CD4 cells for most protein antigens. Activation → clonal expansion → transformation into plasma cells that secrete antibody (humoral immunity) and memory B cells. Humoral handles free toxins and extracellular organisms; cellular handles what hides inside cells. Plasma cells in a section mean a humoral response has run long enough for B cells to have been activated and transformed — one of the three defining cells of chronic inflammation.

The macrophage

The single most important cell in chronic inflammation — and the most dangerous. It digests microbes, engulfs foreign material, presents antigen to T cells (MHC II), and secretes many active substances.

ProductEffect
Reactive oxygen species, nitric oxideToxic to cells (and microbes)
Proteases (MMPs, elastase, collagenase)Toxic to extracellular matrix — dissolve collagen and bone matrix
Cytokines (IL-1, TNF, IL-6, IL-12) and chemokinesRecruit and activate more cells; fever; acute-phase response
Growth factors (PDGF, TGF-β, FGF)Fibrosis — fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition
Growth factors (VEGF, FGF)Angiogenesis

The same cell that kills microbes also dissolves matrix, recruits more inflammatory cells and drives fibrosis — which is why chronic inflammation shows destruction and attempted healing simultaneously. Two populations: tissue residents (diffusely in connective tissue; Kupffer cells in liver, sinus histiocytes in nodes, alveolar macrophages, osteoclast lineage in bone) and the mobile pool of circulating monocytes (half-life 1 day; tissue lifespan months). Monocytes emigrate by the same M-A-D-C sequence, accumulate ~48 hours after the stimulus — which is exactly why acute inflammation lasts a maximum of about 2 days before the picture becomes mononuclear — and are activated by cytokines (IFN-γ), endotoxin or T cells: bigger, more lysosomal enzymes, more active metabolism, better killing. Short-lived stimulus → macrophages disperse (die or drain to nodes). Long-term stimulus → they accumulate by continued recruitment, local proliferation and immobilisation.

Chronic inflammation defined

Chronic inflammation is a prolonged inflammatory response lasting weeks or months, in which tissue damage continues while the body attempts to heal the injured part. In acute inflammation damage and healing are sequential; in chronic inflammation they run simultaneously and indefinitely — which is why histology shows destruction, fibrosis and new vessels in the same field. It happens because of persistent irritation: the body cannot remove or destroy the agent; the agent is resistant (non-digestible, walled in, survives inside macrophages); or the immune response itself sustains it (autoimmunity). Two routes in: following acute inflammation that failed to resolve, or de novo with no acute phase.

AcuteChronic
DurationMinutes to ~2 daysWeeks to months, indefinitely
Cellular infiltrateNeutrophilsMacrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, fibroblasts; ± acute exacerbation superimposed
Vascular changeProminent exudateMinimal exudate; angiogenesis
Tissue damageMild, then healingOngoing destruction — much of it by the host's own inflammatory cells — with simultaneous fibrosis and attempted repair
SystemicFever, leukocytosisLow-grade fever, weight loss, anaemia of chronic disease
Tutorial 3B MCQs 1–2, SAQ 1 live in this table. Neutrophils are not a characteristic cell of chronic inflammation.

The self-sustaining loop

Lymphocytes emigrate by the acute mechanisms, are activated by antigen contact, and produce lymphokines (IFN-γ) that stimulate monocytes and macrophages; macrophage monokines (IL-1, IL-12, TNF) in turn activate lymphocytes and present more antigen. This reciprocal loop is what makes chronic inflammation persist. Plasma cells add antibody, and immune complexes add complement activation. The cells interact: macrophage presents → T cell directs → B cell/plasma cell arms → macrophage destroys.

Causes

CauseDetailExamples
Persistent infectionOrganisms the body cannot clear — low toxicity, survive inside macrophagesTubercle bacilli → TB; Treponema pallidum → syphilis; M. leprae; fungi; viruses (hepatitis B/C)
Prolonged exposure to toxic agentsExogenous or endogenousSilica → silicosis; asbestos; toxic plasma lipid (oxidised LDL) → atherosclerosis
AutoimmunityReactions against the individual's own tissues; autoantigens set up a self-perpetuating reactionRheumatoid arthritis, lupus, Hashimoto
Sterile foreign bodies (de novo)Non-digestible — frustrated phagocytosis continues indefinitelySuture material, implants, amalgam tattoo, retained root fragments
IdiopathicCause unknownSarcoidosis, Crohn's disease, orofacial granulomatosis

Dental relevance. Any material left in the tissues that cannot be digested provokes a chronic response — which is why biocompatibility of dental materials matters and retained foreign bodies are removed.

Histological features and forms

Three things a pathologist looks for: infiltration by mononuclear cells; tissue destruction induced by the inflammatory cells themselves, not only the agent; attempts at healing by connective tissue replacement — angiogenesis and fibrosis. Morphological variants depend on severity, cause, tissue and site. Five named forms follow.

Serous

Outpouring of thin fluid from serum or from the mesothelial lining of peritoneum, pleura or pericardium. A burn or viral blister; pleurisy; pericarditis (often viral); synovitis (viral or autoimmune).

Fibrous (fibrinous)

A more severe injury with greater permeability: fibrin leaks out and a fibrinous exudate forms, characteristic of body cavities. If removed by fibrinolysis and macrophages → resolution. If fibrin is not fully removed it stimulates ingrowth of fibroblasts and vessels that organise it into scar → adhesions, constrictive pericarditis, fibrous ankylosis of the TMJ, rheumatoid arthritis. Pericarditis shows both: serous straw-coloured fluid that may need surgical drainage because the heart cannot beat effectively; if chronic and fibrosed, adhesions and constriction greatly reduce life expectancy. Whether fibrin is cleared decides the outcome.

Suppurative

Large accumulations of pus (neutrophils, necrotic cells, oedema fluid) produced by pyogenic organisms such as staphylococci; abscesses are focal collections buried in tissue. Structure: necrotic pus centre → pyogenic membrane of neutrophils and fibrin → granulation tissue → fibrous wall. Defence cells and drugs cannot reach the centre.

FistulaSinus
A non-epithelial-lined tract (in the lecture's usage), classically joining two epithelial surfaces — oro-antral fistulaAn epithelial-lined channel joining an abscess cavity to an epithelial surface. Allows drainage — and therefore no pain. A pain-free draining sinus from a periapical abscess has not resolved; it has found an escape route and still needs treatment.

Ulcerative

An ulcer is a localised loss of epithelium with exposure of the underlying connective tissue. Causes: continuous physical or chemical injury preventing re-epithelialisation; secondary infection; specific bacteria; immune reactions (ulcerative colitis, vesiculobullous skin disease); and the repair attempt itself. Common outside the mouth in the oesophagus and stomach; inside it, the commonest presentation in oral medicine.

Granulomatous

Characterised by granuloma formation — a grain-like lump: an aggregate of chronic inflammatory cells with tissue damage and destruction. A granuloma is a microscopic aggregate of macrophages transformed into epithelium-like cells, surrounded by a collar of lymphocytes and some plasma cells.

Epithelioid cellsGiant cells
Macrophages that resemble epithelial cells — flat, elongated, oval nucleus, eosinophilic cytoplasm. Unable to phagocytose; release inflammatory and immune mediators. They have given up eating to become secretory.Very large, multinucleate (>50 nuclei); form where macrophages struggle to destroy particles, by fusion — probably accidental. Langhans' giant cell: nuclei in a horseshoe. Foreign-body giant cell: nuclei scattered.

Formation: necrosis in some types (caseous in TB) → walled in by epithelioid cells, macrophages and giant cells → outer zone of lymphocytes and macrophages → maintained by continued release of mediators and toxins (Th1 IFN-γ activating macrophages — this is type IV hypersensitivity, Chapter 6) → granulomata may coalesce with considerable destruction.

CategoryExamples
InfectiousMycobacterial — TB (caseating), leprosy; fungal; treponemal — syphilis (gumma); parasitic
Chemical / foreign bodyTalc, asbestosis, silica; sutures, amalgam
AutoimmuneRheumatoid nodule; Crohn's disease
Unknown / idiopathicSarcoidosis; orofacial granulomatosis (persistent lip or facial swelling); Crohn's also gives oral lesions
Granuloma ≠ granulation tissue. Granulation tissue is the vascular scaffold of healing; a granuloma is a destructive aggregate of chronic inflammatory cells.

Acquired causes of oral lesions — a nine-part scaffold

#CategoryExample
1Physical and chemical agentsCheek biting, aspirin burn, sharp cusp
2Infectious organismsHSV, Candida, TB, syphilis
3Inflammatory processesPeriapical or periodontal inflammation
4Immune diseasesPemphigoid, pemphigus, lichen planus, aphthae
5Nutritional / metabolicB-vitamin, iron, folate deficiency
6NeoplasticSquamous cell carcinoma — the one that must not be missed
7PsychologicalSelf-harm, factitious injury
8IatrogenicNumb lip trauma after LA; instrument injury
9IdiopathicStevens–Johnson syndrome, orofacial granulomatosis

Walk the categories in order for any lesion of unclear cause; 6 and 8 are the most consequential to miss.

Periodontal disease — the model

Periodontal disease is the body's response to plaque bacteria at or below the gum line, inducing inflammation of the gingiva (gingivitis) or the periodontium (periodontitis). It is the second most common cause of tooth loss. Genetic and environmental factors (smoking, diabetes, stress, immune status) raise risk.

  1. Plaque accumulates at the tooth–gingiva interface.
  2. Bacteria release damaging substancesmetabolic acids, extracellular enzymes, lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
  3. Sulcular epithelium and connective tissue are damaged, directly and indirectly.
  4. Mediators are released and the inflammatory response is activated.
Gingivitis — acute inflammation in the mouthPeriodontitis — chronic inflammation in the mouth
EventsVessels dilate, permeability increases, leukocytes migrate — the three tissue events of Chapter 3. Neutrophils form a barrier between plaque and crevicular epithelium and phagocytose some bacteria (not a critical control mechanism).Large infiltrate of macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells — the mononuclear picture. Bacterial and host damage to the tissues.
HistologyInflammation confined to gingival connective tissue; junctional epithelium at the CEJ; no attachment or bone loss; reversible.Apical migration and ulceration of junctional epithelium → pocket; destruction of collagen and PDL by host MMPs; osteoclast activation (IL-1, TNF, RANKL) → alveolar bone loss; fibrosis; irreversible attachment loss.
Cardinal signsRed, swollen gingiva = rubor + tumor · raised intra-crevicular temperature = calor · pain on probing = dolor · papilla no longer deflects food debris = functio laesa

Why it never resolves. Plaque sits on a non-shedding, non-vascularised surface that is technically outside the body — the immune system cannot reach it, the stop condition is never met, and the host's own response destroys the supporting tissues. Mechanical plaque removal, not immunity or antibiotics, is therefore the definitive treatment. Periodontal abscess: if the neutrophil influx is overwhelmed, degranulation of many neutrophils in a confined space attacks host tissue (the self-harm mechanism from Chapter 3); or blockage of the crevicular orifice stops gingival crevicular fluid draining — pressure builds, exactly as with a blocked sinus.

Tutorial 3B scenario: persistent gingivitis despite hygiene → progression driven by plaque retention the patient cannot reach (pockets, calculus), host susceptibility (genetics, smoking, diabetes), and a shift to a dysbiotic anaerobic flora. Histological difference: neutrophil-dominated, no attachment loss vs mononuclear, pocket, PDL and bone loss.

Drill

Describe the roles of macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells in chronic inflammation and how they interact.

Macrophages phagocytose, present antigen on MHC II, and secrete ROS/NO and proteases (destruction), cytokines (recruitment) and growth factors (fibrosis, angiogenesis). CD4 lymphocytes recognise the presented antigen and release cytokines — IFN-γ activates macrophages, IL-4/5 help B cells; CD8 cells kill infected cells. B cells activated by antigen become plasma cells that secrete antibody, opsonising targets and fixing complement. Macrophage → T cell → B/plasma cell → macrophage is a reciprocal loop that persists until the antigen is gone.

Why must a cytotoxic T cell recognise MHC class I rather than class II?

Class I is displayed by every nucleated cell, so an infected or transformed cell anywhere in the body can present its abnormal peptides. The CD8 cell's job is to kill such cells, so it must read the molecule ordinary cells carry. Class II is restricted to antigen-presenting cells and is read by CD4 helpers, whose job is to direct rather than kill.

Two patients have pericarditis. One recovers fully; the other develops constrictive pericarditis. What decided it?

Whether the fibrinous exudate was removed. Cleared by fibrinolysis and macrophages → resolution. Not fully cleared → fibrin stimulates fibroblast and vessel ingrowth that organises it into scar → adhesions and constriction, greatly reducing life expectancy.

Why is an abscess difficult to treat with antibiotics alone?

It is walled off by granulation tissue with a necrotic, avascular centre; defence cells and blood-borne drugs cannot reach the pus reliably. Release of pus (drainage) is what allows organisation and healing.

Tutorial 3B — answer key

MCQ — chronic inflammation is characterised by
c) Prolonged duration and tissue damage.
MCQ — NOT a characteristic cell
d) Neutrophils.
MCQ — key mediator from activated CD4+ cells
c) Cytokines.
SAQ — acute vs chronic
Duration: ≤2 days vs weeks–months. Infiltrate: neutrophils vs macrophages/lymphocytes/plasma cells. Damage: mild then healing vs ongoing host-mediated destruction with simultaneous fibrosis.
SAQ — macrophage, lymphocyte, plasma cell roles
Macrophage: phagocytosis, antigen presentation, ROS/proteases/cytokines/growth factors. Lymphocytes: CD4 cytokine direction, CD8 killing, lymphokine–monokine loop. Plasma cells: antibody. Reciprocal activation sustains the lesion.
Scenario — gingivitis → periodontitis
Plaque cannot be removed by the host (outside the body, non-shedding surface); persistent LPS/antigen + susceptible host → shift from neutrophil/acute to mononuclear/chronic; host MMPs and RANKL destroy PDL and bone. Gingivitis: confined, JE at CEJ, reversible. Periodontitis: pocket, attachment and bone loss, mononuclear infiltrate, fibrosis.
