Chapter 5 · Tutorial 4

Healing and Repair

Regeneration, organisation, wound healing, bone, and the tooth socket

Inflammation clears the damage; this chapter is about what fills the gap. Whether a tissue truly heals or is merely patched with scar depends on the cells it is made of, whether the stem-cell niche survived, and how much tissue was lost.

Know these cold

  • Underwood's: healing = regeneration; repair = organisation (scar). Robbins uses 'healing' for both
  • Labile cells have the highest regenerative capacity
  • First vs second intention: same steps, different amount of tissue lost
  • EGF → epithelium; PDGF → fibroblasts; TGF-β → collagen/myofibroblasts; VEGF → vessels
  • Wound contraction = myofibroblasts
  • Socket: 4 h clot retraction; dry-socket risk peaks ~2 days; bone at 18 days; lamellar at 6 weeks
  • Steroids act twice; diabetes hits everything

Cell types and stem cells

Whether a tissue can heal at all is decided before the injury happens. Labile cells (epidermis, oral mucosa, gut lining, marrow) divide throughout life and have the highest regenerative capacity; stable cells (liver, kidney, fibroblasts) divide when needed; permanent cells (neurons, cardiac and skeletal muscle) divide only in foetal life and are replaced by scar.

A stem cell retains the ability to divide and, in the fullest case, to form a complete organism; stem cells are the reservoir labile and stable tissues draw on. Two properties: self-renewal and differentiation. How many types they can become is potency, which narrows one-way during development:

GradeCan formNote
TotipotentAll cells of the embryo and the placentaThe only grade that includes supporting tissue — zygote, first cleavages
PluripotentAll cells of the three germ layers, but not extra-embryonic tissueEctoderm, mesoderm, endoderm — embryonic stem cells
MultipotentA number of cell types within one lineageHaematopoietic stem cell; mesenchymal stem cell
UnipotentOne cell typeStill self-renewing — that keeps it a stem cell

Stem cells sit in protected niches, furthest from the surface being worn away: the basal layer of epidermis, the base of intestinal crypts. Daughter cells migrate outward as they mature and are shed. A superficial abrasion spares the niche and regenerates without scar; a deep burn destroys it and must scar, with epithelium creeping in only from surviving margins.

Dentistry. The periodontium (cementum, PDL, alveolar bone) does not regenerate on its own once destroyed by periodontitis; conventional treatment arrests disease but yields repair — a long junctional epithelium — not a new attachment. Periodontal regenerative therapy and tissue engineering (Han et al. 2014) aim to move the outcome from the repair column into the healing column.

Healing versus repair

Healing (regeneration)Repair (organisation)
Complete restoration with no or minimal residual defect. Part of a labile/stable cell population is lost, but the tissue that returns is the tissue that was there. Requires: cells able to divide, and an intact stromal framework.Restoration with fibrovascular connective tissue, with loss of specialised cell populations. The gap is filled with something less capable than the original — a scar. Occurs when cells are permanent, the framework is destroyed, or tissue loss is large.
Terminology trap, flagged by the lecturer. Robbins: "healing" = umbrella for regeneration + repair. Underwood's (this course): "healing" = regeneration, the opposite of repair. Check which convention a question uses.

Healing: the process (abrasion)

  1. Normal skinintact epidermis over an intact basement membrane.
  2. Abrasionsurface layers scraped away; basal layer survives.
  3. Scab formsa layer of fibrin that protects the epidermis as it grows to cover the gap underneath. Epithelium migrates beneath the scab, not over it — the same principle that makes the clot matter in a socket.
  4. Cells proliferate and migrate from the edges as a thin sheet until the defect is covered.
  5. Proliferation stops once the sheet is confluent — contact inhibition.
  6. The epidermis is rebuilt from the base upward to full thickness.

Contact inhibition: cells stop proliferating when they come into contact with one another. It halts regeneration at exactly the right moment. In neoplasia this control is lost, allowing continued proliferation of tumour cells — the same machinery that makes ordered healing possible, failing.

Organisation: the process (repair)

Organisation is the repair of specialised tissues by the formation of mature fibrovascular connective tissue — the process that produces a scar.

  1. Fibrin depositiona provisional scaffold fills the defect.
  2. Granulation tissuenew capillaries and fibroblasts grow into the fibrin (with macrophages, in a loose matrix). This is the same tissue met in acute inflammation; it is not a granuloma and not pus.
  3. Removal of dead tissue by neutrophils and macrophages.
  4. Contraction of the granulation tissue reduces the volume to be filled.
  5. Collagen accumulates to form the scar — type III first, remodelled to type I over months; strength never reaches that of the original, and elastic fibres are not reconstructed.

Wound contraction and scarring

Contraction reduces the volume of tissue to be repaired — helpful at first. It results from the contraction of myofibroblasts in the granulation tissue, which are attached to each other and to the matrix, so the whole wound bed is drawn inward. Infection and its inflammation increase scarring — wound infection has a lasting cost. Excess contraction causes stenosis (stricture of a tube lumen — oesophagus, bile duct, bowel), contracture (permanent shortening of a muscle, limiting movement) and cosmetic and functional loss after burns.

Tutorial 4 MCQ 4: wound contraction is mediated by myofibroblasts — not fibroblasts.

Skin: first and second intention

First intention is the pattern of surgical incisions: very little damage on either side of the cut, and close approximation of the edges enables prompt, uneventful healing. Incision → the narrow gap fills with fibrin and a scab/eschar forms → capillaries proliferate across the line → fibroblasts migrate into the fibrin and secrete collagen → epithelium bridges the gap within 24–48 h. Even here the elastic fibre network is never reconstructed — a fine scar remains detectably different from surrounding skin.

Second intention deals with a defect, not a line: tissue loss, gaping margins that cannot be apposed, and more haemorrhage and infection because a large open surface bleeds and is colonised. Phagocytosis of debris → abundant granulation tissue fills the defect from the base up → epithelium migrates only once there is a bed to migrate over → marked contraction.

First intentionSecond intention
Typical causeSurgical incision, sutured lacerationTissue loss — ulcer, avulsion, burn, extraction socket
Wound edgesClosely apposedGaping
Tissue lostMinimalSubstantial
InflammationMinimalMore intense, longer
Granulation tissueScantAbundant — must fill the defect
EpithelialisationRapid — 24–48 h bridgeSlow — only once a bed exists
ContractionLittleMarked
Infection riskLowHigh
ScarSmall, linearLarge, liable to contract

The difference is not the mechanism — both use the same steps — but the amount of tissue lost, and therefore how much granulation tissue is needed. Everything else follows.

Tutorial 4 scenarios. Biopsy incision → first intention: clean, minimal loss, edges approximated by sutures. Large deep leg laceration with tissue loss → second intention: broad contracted scar, slower, infection-prone. Both ask what impairs healing — see the last section.

Mechanism: cytokines and growth factors

A complex interplay, with two rules: the same cell produces many cytokines, and most cytokines have many functions. Initiating signals are hypoxia (the centre of a defect is hypoxic once its supply is cut — the wound signals its own need for vessels) and growth factors from platelet degranulation.

FactorSourceMain job
EGF / KGFPlatelets, macrophages, fibroblasts (KGF from fibroblasts)Keratinocyte proliferation and migration — epithelial regeneration
PDGFPlatelets, macrophages, keratinocytes, endotheliumChemotaxis and proliferation of fibroblasts and smooth muscle; macrophage activation; matrix production
VEGFKeratinocytes, macrophages (hypoxia-driven)Angiogenesis — endothelial proliferation, migration, permeability
FGFMacrophages, fibroblastsAngiogenesis, fibroblast proliferation, keratinocyte migration
TGF-βPlatelets, macrophages, fibroblastsControls myofibroblasts and collagen formation — fibrosis, scarring; anti-inflammatory
IL-1 / TNFMacrophagesRecruit inflammatory cells, induce MMPs, fever

Angiogenesis: VEGF and PDGF together drive macrophage activation, fibroblast proliferation and matrix production — the three things that turn an empty defect into granulation tissue. New vessels are leaky (one of the five permeability mechanisms in Chapter 3).

Abnormal scars

Hypertrophic scarKeloid
ExtentStays within the original wound boundaryGrows beyond the original wound boundary
CourseOften regressesPersists; commonly recurs after excision; darker skin, earlobes, sternum
CauseExcess collagen deposition under abnormal TGF-β control

Mucosal ulcers

Bleeding, then covering by fibrin (the protective layer) → removal of necrotic tissue by macrophages → granulation tissue fills the base → epithelial regeneration from the ulcer edges — epithelium can only advance from surviving margins, so a wide ulcer takes disproportionately long. Chronic ulceration (cause not removed) enters a cycle of alternating ulceration and repair with ongoing destruction; fibrous scar replaces muscle and contracts — stenosis in a hollow organ such as the stomach. This is the histological counterpart of ulcerative inflammation in Chapter 4.

Bone

Bone is exceptional: a specialised tissue that regenerates as bone, through a temporary weaker form.

  1. Haematomablood from periosteal and marrow vessels fills the fracture; it is organised and dead bone removed; inflammatory cells and then granulation tissue arrive.
  2. Callus — woven boneinternal and external callus of woven bone, laid down in an irregular pattern: quick to make, mechanically weak; osteoblasts from periosteum and endosteum, with cartilage where oxygen is low.
  3. Lamellar bone and remodellingwoven bone replaced by lamellar bone and remodelled according to the direction of mechanical stress; medullary cavity restored.
FactorConsequence
MobilityFibrous union — a false joint (pseudarthrosis); movement stops the callus mineralising into a bony bridge — the reason fractures are immobilised
Interposed soft tissueNon-union — tissue physically blocks the bone ends
MisalignmentMalunion; impaired function; osteoarthrosis in adjacent joints
InfectionPrevents or delays union (osteomyelitis; compound fractures)
Pre-existing bone diseaseCompromises the response — osteoporosis, Paget's, MRONJ, irradiated bone

Pathological fracture: from disease of bone — primary disorder or secondary involvement (metastasis, cyst, tumour); the bone fails under a load it should tolerate. In the mandible: MRONJ, osteomyelitis, radiotherapy, large cysts or tumours. Compound fracture: involves the overlying skin — exposed, hence high infection risk. Distraction osteogenesis: healing exploited deliberately — bone cut and segments slowly separated so new bone forms in the gap; used to lengthen the jaw.

Liver, nerve and muscle

TissueResponse
LiverThree sources of regeneration: hepatocytes re-entering the cycle (stable cells), resident liver progenitor cells, bone-marrow-derived stem cells. Regenerates functioning parenchyma if the framework survives; chronic injury → cirrhosis (fibrosis with nodular regeneration).
CNSDoes not repair effectively. Adult neurons have low replicative capacity; the response is gliosis — glial proliferation that fills the defect without restoring function. The CNS equivalent of scarring.
Peripheral nerveArchitecture matters: epineurium (outer), perineurium (around fascicles), endoneurium (around individual fibres). If the sheath is intact the axon distal to injury degenerates (Wallerian) and the proximal axon regrows along the tube ~1 mm/day; if the sheath is severed, regrowth is disordered — neuroma, paraesthesia. Relevant to lingual/inferior alveolar nerve injury.
Cardiac musclePermanent — replaced by scar; permanent functional deficit after infarct
Smooth musclePermanent, but vascular smooth muscle differs in that new vessels can form
Skeletal muscleLimited regeneration from satellite cells; if only contractile proteins are lost and the fibre survives, new ones can be synthesised inside the old endomysium — refitted, not replaced

The tooth socket

Immediately: normal clotting produces a loose clot filling the bony and soft-tissue socket. Platelets retract it, expressing fluid so it hardens and shrinks below the soft-tissue margin, pulling mobile soft tissue inward to reduce exposed clot. Clot retraction is usually complete in 4 hours and the surface changes from shiny to matt; fibrin cross-linking continues to stabilise it — which is why no rinsing for 24 hours.

TimeWhat is happening
4 hoursClot retraction complete; shiny → matt; fibrin cross-linking
2 daysFibrinolysis has started; inflammatory cells emigrate into the clot. Clot poorly anchored → peak dry-socket risk
4 daysMacrophages remove debris; organisation begins; bacterial enzymes lyse surface fibrin; epithelium starts to grow beneath surface debris over the intact clot
8 daysSocket filled with granulation tissue; superficial inflammatory cells; lamina dura intact but resorption begun
18 daysCollagen deposition; woven bone forming; osteogenic front advancing
6 weeksRemodelling to lamellar bone; lamina dura still visible radiographically

Dry socket (alveolar osteitis): loss or lysis of the clot exposing bare bone — severe pain from day 2–4, halitosis, empty socket. Risk factors: smoking, oral contraceptives, traumatic extraction, mandibular molars, prior infection, rinsing/sucking. The timing follows the table: fibrinolysis has begun but the clot is not yet anchored to the wall. The socket combines bone healing underneath with epithelial regeneration on top, over a clot that must be protected.

Factors that affect healing

FactorWhy it impairs healing
AgeReduced capacity and cellular reserves; thinner skin, poorer perfusion
NutritionProtein for collagen; vitamin C for hydroxylation of collagen; zinc for enzymes; deficiency → weak, delayed repair
Neoplastic disordersCompete for resources; impair the general response; cachexia
Cushing's / steroid therapyActs twice: immunosuppression makes infection more severe, and steroids directly interfere with granulation-tissue formation and therefore contraction
Diabetes & immunosuppressionSeveral mechanisms at once — infection, immune suppression, impaired neutrophil function, ischaemia (micro/macroangiopathy), neuropathy
Vascular disturbanceNo perfusion → no oxygen, cells or substrate; venous stasis ulcers, arterial disease, irradiated tissue
DenervationUnresponsive to repeated minor trauma; no pain from infection → injury unnoticed and unprotected
LocalInfection, foreign body, mobility, size and depth of defect, poor apposition, radiation, mechanical stress
OtherSmoking (vasoconstriction, hypoxia), psychological stress (Guo & DiPietro), alcohol, some drugs (chemotherapy, NSAIDs at high dose)

Diabetes is the standard case because it hits every requirement simultaneously — perfusion, defence, and protection (neuropathy removes the pain that would prompt offloading).

Drill

Why is woven bone laid down first if lamellar bone is stronger?

Because it can be produced quickly. Woven bone bridges the fracture and gives provisional stability far sooner than organised bone could; it is then replaced by lamellar bone and remodelled to the direction of load. Speed first, strength second.

A patient undergoes a surgical biopsy. Describe the expected healing, why it is first intention, and what could impair it.

Clean incision, minimal collateral damage, edges approximated by suture → fibrin fills the narrow cleft, scab forms → capillaries bud across, fibroblasts secrete collagen → epithelium bridges in 24–48 h → collagen matures over weeks into a fine linear scar; elastin not restored. First intention because tissue loss is minimal and edges are apposed. Impaired by: infection, haematoma, tension or mobility, foreign material, poor perfusion, smoking, diabetes, steroids, malnutrition, age, radiation.

Why does the CNS scar so badly, and what is the CNS "scar" called?

Neurons are permanent cells with very low replicative capacity. The defect is filled by proliferating glial cells — gliosis — which restores structure but not function.

Give two distinct mechanisms by which corticosteroids impair wound healing.

Immunosuppression — infection and its consequences are more severe. Direct interference with granulation-tissue formation — and therefore with contraction, since contraction depends on the myofibroblasts within it.

Tutorial 4 — answer key

MCQ — highest regenerative capacity
c) Labile cells.

SAQ — healing vs repair
Healing/regeneration: restoration by the same specialised cells, no residual defect, needs dividing cells + intact stroma. Repair/organisation: fibrovascular tissue → scar, specialised cells lost. Note Robbins vs Underwood's usage.
SAQ — classify tissues by regenerative capacity

Scenario — biopsy incision
First intention as above; impaired by infection, tension/mobility, foreign body, poor perfusion, smoking, diabetes, steroids, nutrition, age, radiation.
Scenario — large deep laceration
Second intention as above; outcome differs by broad contracted scar, longer time, contracture risk, infection risk; muscle and nerve may not regenerate.

Chapter 6 · Tutorial 5a

Immunopathology 1 — Hypersensitivity

Four mechanisms, three antibody-driven and one cell-driven; two of them can kill a patient in the chair

The immune system doing exactly what it was built to do, and injuring the host in the process. Every mechanism here was built in Chapter 4 — only the outcome is different.

Know these cold

  • Hypersensitivity = incidental tissue injury from a response aimed at foreign antigen
  • I: IgE–mast cell, minutes · II: IgG/IgM on cell-bound antigen · III: immune complexes of soluble antigen · IV: T cells, 2–3 days
  • Th2 → IL-4 (IgE), IL-5 (eosinophils), IL-13 (mucus); cross-linking of IgE on FcεRI is the trigger
  • Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 300 µg (150 µg <5 y), repeat every 5 min, ambulance
  • Myasthenia (blocks AChR) vs Graves (stimulates TSHR); SLE anti-dsDNA/anti-Sm specific
  • Skin-prick = type I; patch test at 2 and 4 days = type IV. Chlorhexidine does both

Definition and causes

A hypersensitivity reaction is incidental tissue injury as a result of the immune response intended to destroy foreign antigens. The word that matters is incidental: the response is working; the damage is collateral — aimed at the wrong target, out of proportion, or unable to stop.

Source of antigenDetail
AutoimmunityResponse directed at a self antigen — Chapter 7.
MicrobesThree ways: an excessive reaction; a persistent microbe (M. tuberculosis); or cross-reactivity with self — rheumatic heart disease: antibodies raised against streptococcal antigens also bind cardiac tissue because the two are structurally similar (molecular mimicry).
Environmental antigensIn genetically susceptible individuals; ~20% of the population are allergic to something. Atopy = an inherited tendency to over-produce IgE to common environmental antigens — the tendency, not the disease.
Tutorial 5a MCQ 1: hypersensitivity = c) immune responses that cause tissue damage. SAQ 1: definition + the three sources with examples.

The four types (Gell and Coombs)

TypeNameMediated byCore eventTimingExamples
IImmediateIgE on mast cellsAntigen cross-links IgE → degranulationMinutesAnaphylaxis, urticaria, hay fever, asthma, food allergy
IIAntibody to cell-bound antigenIgM / IgG ± complementAntibody binds an antigen fixed on a cell membrane → lysis, phagocytosis, or receptor block/stimulationHoursTransfusion reaction, haemolytic anaemia, myasthenia gravis, Graves, pemphigoid
IIIImmune complexIgG + complementAntibody binds soluble antigen → complexes deposit in vessels, joints, glomeruliHours–daysSLE, post-streptococcal GN, serum sickness, vasculitis
IVDelayed (cell-mediated)Sensitised T cellsTh1/CD8 react on re-exposure; macrophage activation2–3 daysContact dermatitis, TB granuloma, type 1 diabetes, transplant rejection, Sjögren

Types I–III are antibody-mediated; IV is cell-mediated — which is why IV is the only delayed one: antibody is already circulating and acts in minutes; T cells must migrate to the site, which takes days. Types II and III are both IgG: what separates them is where the antigen is — fixed to a cell (damage confined to that tissue) or soluble (complexes travel and lodge wherever flow slows, so disease is multi-system).

Tutorial 5a MCQ 2: type III = c) immune complexes deposited in tissues.

Type I — mechanism

Often called allergy or atopy; the commonest disorder of the immune system.

  1. Initial exposureantigen (pollen, peanut, penicillin, latex; a protein or a chemical bound to protein) reaches an epithelial surface and is presented to CD4 cells, driving a strong Th2 response.
  2. Class switching to IgEIL-4 (and IL-13) from Th2 cells make B cells switch to IgE-secreting plasma cells; IL-5 activates eosinophils; IL-13 stimulates mucus secretion.
  3. Mast-cell sensitisationIgE binds via its Fc (ε chain) to FcεRI on mast cells (also basophils, eosinophils). Mast cells sit in connective tissue under epithelia and beside vessels — exactly where allergen arrives. Steps 1–3 are clinically silent.
  4. Repeat exposure cross-links IgEantigen bridges two or more adjacent IgE molecules, clustering receptors. A single IgE binding does nothing; cross-linking is the trigger — so tiny amounts of multivalent allergen provoke a massive response.
  5. Immediate phase (minutes)degranulation of preformed mediators: histamine (vasodilation, ↑ permeability, smooth-muscle contraction, mucus), proteases, chemokines, heparin.
  6. Late phase (2–24 h)newly synthesised lipid mediators (leukotrienes, PGD₂, PAF) and cytokines (TNF, IL-4/5) recruit eosinophils, neutrophils, Th2 cells; their proteases cause further tissue damage; sustained bronchospasm and oedema.
"He's had penicillin before without trouble" is not reassurance — prior exposure is the precondition for a type I reaction. IL-4 → IgE (four letters); IL-5 → eosinophils; IL-13 → mucus.
MediatorTypeEffects
HistaminePreformedVasodilation, increased permeability, smooth-muscle contraction, mucus secretion, itch
Proteases (tryptase, chymase)PreformedTissue damage; generate kinins; activate complement → more chemotaxis
Chemokines / TNFPreformedAttract neutrophils and eosinophils
Prostaglandin D₂Newly synthesised (COX)Most abundant COX product of mast cells; intense bronchospasm, mucus
Leukotrienes C4, D4 (E4)Newly synthesised (LOX)The most potent vasoactive and spasmogenic agents known — several thousand times histamine at permeability and bronchoconstriction
Leukotriene B4Newly synthesisedHighly chemotactic for neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes
PAFNewly synthesisedPlatelet aggregation, bronchospasm, permeability

Antihistamines fail in severe asthma and the late phase because histamine is one preformed mediator; leukotrienes and PGD₂ act later, are far more potent, and are not blocked by an H1 antagonist. Complement amplifies: mast-cell proteases activate it, C3a/C4a/C5a (anaphylatoxins) increase permeability, release vasoactive amines and cause smooth-muscle spasm, and C5a is a potent chemoattractant. Complement is the common amplifier across types I, II and III.

Anaphylaxis

Sudden hypotension, severe bronchoconstriction and collapse — a systemic type I reaction. Common triggers: bee and wasp venom, antimicrobials (penicillin), peanuts and nuts, latex, contrast media. The word is Greek for "backwards protection". Anaphylactoid reactions release the same mediators without IgE (direct mast-cell activation by drugs, contrast) — clinically identical, treated identically, can occur on first exposure.

In dental practice: 0.004–0.015 cases per dentist per year — rare enough you may never see one, frequent enough you must be ready. Dental causes: latex, topical preparations (povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine), oil of cloves, penicillins, NSAIDs, occasionally local anaesthetic additives. Chlorhexidine irrigation of a socket puts it into an open vascular bed — fatal anaphylaxis has been reported.

SystemFeaturesMechanism
SkinUrticaria, angioedema, flushing, pruritusHistamine → vasodilation and permeability
RespiratoryStridor, wheeze, dyspnoea, upper-airway angioedema, persistent cough, rhinorrhoeaLaryngeal oedema; bronchial smooth-muscle contraction (LTC4/D4, PGD₂); mucus
CardiovascularHypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmia, syncopeMassive vasodilation plus fluid shift out of vessels → distributive shock
CNSDizziness, confusion, sense of doom, unconsciousnessHypoperfusion
GITNausea, vomiting, cramps, diarrhoeaSmooth-muscle contraction

Management

DeviceDoseUse
EpiPen / Anapen300 µg adrenaline IM (lateral thigh)Adults and children over 5
EpiPen Jr / Anapen 150150 µgUnder 5 years
Anapen 500500 µgSome patients are prescribed this

Repeat every 5 minutes if symptoms persist; a single dose is the first dose, not the treatment. Call an ambulance at the same time. Lie the patient flat with legs raised (sit up only if breathing is the main problem), give high-flow oxygen, remove the trigger, monitor. Adrenaline reverses the three things killing the patient — α₁ vasoconstriction (hypotension), β₂ bronchodilation (bronchospasm), and mast-cell stabilisation via β₂. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts, acting late or on one mediator only; leukotrienes alone would be enough to kill.

Tutorial 5a scenario (bee sting): venom cross-links IgE on sensitised mast cells → histamine, leukotrienes, PGD₂, PAF → hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema, urticaria, GI upset → first-line: IM adrenaline, repeat at 5 min, call ambulance.

Type II — antibody to cell-bound antigen

Antibodies (IgM or IgG) react with antigenic determinants that form part of the cell membrane of the target tissue; complement and accessory cells may be involved.

MechanismHowExample
Direct inflammatory attack / complement lysisAntibody fixes complement → membrane-attack complex lysis and C5a-driven inflammation confined to the tissue carrying the antigenMucous membrane pemphigoid (basement-membrane zone → sub-epithelial blisters, desquamative gingivitis); transfusion reaction; Goodpasture
Opsonisation and phagocytosis (± ADCC)Antibody/C3b-coated cells are removed by splenic macrophages or killed by NK cellsAutoimmune haemolytic anaemia, immune thrombocytopenia, haemolytic disease of the newborn
Receptor interferenceAntibody binds a receptor and either inhibits it or mimics the ligand and activates itMyasthenia gravis — anti-AChR blocks neuromuscular transmission → weakness. Graves disease — anti-TSH-receptor stimulates thyroid without TSH → thyrotoxicosis (sometimes called type V because it stimulates rather than destroys)

Drugs and bystander lysis. Many type II reactions involve drugs or metabolites (penicillin, quinidine, methyldopa) bound to red cells or platelets, forming highly immunogenic epitopes. Antibody raised against the drug inadvertently destroys the cell it is stuck to — drug-induced haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenic purpura. The same mechanism operates against intrinsic self antigens with no drug involved.

Tutorial 5a SAQ 3: three type II mechanisms (lysis, opsonisation, receptor interference) + two diseases — pick myasthenia gravis and Graves, or haemolytic anaemia and pemphigoid.

Type III — immune complexes

Antibodies target soluble antigens, forming immune complexes that fix complement and are not cleared from the circulation. The complexes deposit in blood vessels, joints and glomeruli — wherever the circulation narrows or filters — and induce a local inflammatory response. Because the complex travels, type III disease is characteristically multi-system regardless of where the antigen came from.

  1. High concentration of complexes deposits in vessel wall or basement membrane (favoured by intermediate size, slight antigen excess, high pressure and filtration).
  2. Complement activationC3a and C5a generated.
  3. Platelet aggregation → local vascular obstruction, micro-thrombi.
  4. Neutrophil attraction by C5a; frustrated phagocytosis of fixed complexes releases enzymes onto the wall.
  5. Local inflammation and tissue damagefibrinoid necrosis of vessels (vasculitis), glomerulonephritis, arthritis.

Chronic complex formation occurs with persistent antigen exposure (chronic infection, autoantigen), an abnormal host response, or local defects such as complement deficiency (poor clearance).

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

Streptococcal throat or skin infection → 10–12 days for antibody to form complexes → antigenic fragments of nephritogenic strains bind the glomerular basement membrane → IgG and C3 deposits → inflammation and renal injury (haematuria, oedema, hypertension). A one-shot mechanism — a single burst after one infection, so it usually resolves once antigen is cleared, unlike SLE which relapses indefinitely. A fortnight's latent period after a sore throat is the exam signal for type III.

Systemic lupus erythematosus

Multisystem inflammation from abnormal immune function, with flares and remissions. Type III: immune complexes of anti-nuclear antibodies with nuclear antigens deposit in tissue, activate complement, and cause inflammation. Four types: systemic; neonatal (maternal antibody); discoid (skin and oral mucosa only — chronic scarring atrophic lesions that may progress); drug-induced (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid — resolves on cessation over days to months).

EpidemiologyIncidence (US) 2–8/100,000; prevalence (Australia) 45/100,000, higher in Indigenous Australians; female predominance, child-bearing age
AetiologyMultifactorial. Genetics: >100 loci, each small effect; 25% monozygotic vs 2–5% dizygotic concordance. Environmental: EBV, UV light, smoking, drugs. Hormonal: oestrogen. Defective clearance of apoptotic cells exposes nuclear antigen.
SkinMalar (butterfly) rash sparing the nasolabial folds; photosensitivity; discoid lesions; alopecia; Raynaud's. Oral: discoid-like white/red lesions, ulcers on palate and buccal mucosa, lichenoid change
MusculoskeletalArthralgia, myalgia, non-erosive arthritis
RenalLupus nephritis — the main cause of morbidity
CardiopulmonaryPericarditis, myocarditis, Libman–Sacks endocarditis, accelerated coronary disease; pleuritis, pleuritic pain
HaematologicalAnaemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia; antiphospholipid antibodies → thrombosis
DiagnosisNo consensus set; ACR 1997: 11 criteria, 4 of 11 diagnostic, at least one clinical and one immunological (sensitivity 95%, specificity 85%). ANA almost always positive but not specific; anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm highly specific; anti-C1q tracks activity; low complement in flares

Dental: oral ulceration and lichenoid lesions, xerostomia (secondary Sjögren), increased infection and bleeding risk on immunosuppressants and antiphospholipid therapy, steroid cover, Libman–Sacks valve lesions and endocarditis risk, photosensitivity of the lips.

Type IV — delayed-type hypersensitivity

  1. Sensitisationantigen (hapten–carrier) is taken up by Langerhans/dendritic cells, carried to the node and presented on MHC II to CD4 cells → memory Th1 (and Th17) cells. Silent, often months after small exposures.
  2. Re-exposuresensitised T cells recognise the antigen at the site and release IL-2, IFN-γ, TNF and other Th1 cytokines.
  3. Adhesion molecules up-regulatedTNF induces ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 on endothelium (the Chapter 3 cascade).
  4. Extravasation of monocytes, macrophages, neutrophils, more T cells; IFN-γ activates macrophages.
  5. Tissue damageincreased permeability → oedema; macrophage enzymes and ROS → necrosis; if antigen persists, epithelioid cells and giant cells → granuloma.
  6. Timingeffector T cells take 24–48 h to migrate; reaction clinically evident at 2–3 days, peak 48–72 h, then declines.
CellAction
CD4+Release cytokines that initiate local inflammation and activate macrophages. Th1 → IFN-γ → macrophages (the granuloma engine); Th17 → IL-17 → neutrophils. Main effectors of tissue damage
CD8+Kill antigen-bearing cells directly (perforin/granzyme, Fas) — contact dermatitis, viral hepatitis, type 1 diabetes β-cell loss
BothPresent together in many conditions

Causes: autoimmunity (type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren, Hashimoto) and environmental antigens with an exaggerated or persistent response (contact dermatitis, TB, leprosy, viral hepatitis, transplant rejection). The macrophage–lymphocyte loop of chronic inflammation is this mechanism: TB is both a chronic granulomatous infection and a type IV reaction.

Contact dermatitis

Occupational and other antigens (nickel, chromate, rubber accelerators, fragrances, poison ivy urushiol) are not immunogenic alone: they are reactive haptens that bind skin proteins to become immunogenic. Induction: Langerhans cells present hapten–carrier on MHC II to T cells — usually months after small exposures. Elicitation: on re-exposure effector T cells migrate to the epidermis, meet the complex on Langerhans cells, release cytokines → inflammation at 12–48 h. Clinical: papular erythematous plaques, vesicles, scaling, fissuring in the distribution of exposure with poorly defined margins; hands most often, also face, lips, eyelids. Histology: spongiosis (keratinocytes separated by oedema), lymphocyte exocytosis, superficial perivascular lymphocytes and eosinophils; chronic → epithelial hyperplasia. Management: avoid the allergen (definitive), patch test to identify it, skin care (avoid detergents, emollients), mild topical steroids; short oral steroids for acute facial disease.

Irritant ≠ allergic. Only allergic contact dermatitis is type IV. Irritant dermatitis is direct chemical damage with no memory — first contact, anyone.

Oral contact allergy

A type IV reaction in the oral mucosa; may present as an oral lichenoid reaction. Symptoms: burning, stinging, tingling, xerostomia, dysgeusia. Signs: erythema, oedema, desquamation, ulceration of tongue, gingiva and lining mucosa; cheilitis and peri-oral inflammation.

GroupExamples
Restorative materialsAmalgam, composite resins, acrylics (residual monomer), cements
MetalsNickel sulphate, gold sodium thiosulfate, mercury and amalgam alloy components, chromium–cobalt, palladium chloride
Flavouring agentsCinnamon (cinnamic aldehyde), peppermint, spearmint, fragrance mix, balsam of Peru
Other toothpaste / rinse componentsCocamidopropyl betaine, propylene glycol, parabens, sodium laureth sulphate, triclosan, chlorhexidine

Toothpaste allergy is uncommon and less common than it was because formulations dropped cinnamon; the commonest presentation is cheilitis — dry, red, swollen, cracked lips ± angular cheilitis — often without intra-oral signs. The diagnostic catch: the allergen is usually listed only as "unspecified flavouring", patch testing may not confirm it and a positive may not be clinically relevant, so the lecture's method is stop–restart: withdraw the product, see if it resolves, reintroduce, see if it recurs. Management: establish a temporal relationship; assess symptoms, signs and patch tests; remove the cause (replace restorations, change products); topical steroids for symptoms; and if chlorhexidine anaphylaxis, adrenaline and ambulance. Amalgam-associated lichenoid lesions resolve on replacing the contacting restoration.

Chlorhexidine does both: burning mouth after a rinse = type IV; collapse after socket irrigation = type I.

Patch testing

Apply suspected sensitisers to normal skin on the back under occlusion for 48 hours; read at day 2 and day 4; a positive shows erythema, induration and vesicles. The timings exist because this is a delayed reaction — reading at 20 minutes tells you nothing. Skin-prick test, read in minutes for weal and flare = type I. Patch test, read at 2–4 days for induration = type IV. If a question tells you the test, it has told you the type.

Drill

Explain the pathogenesis of type I hypersensitivity, naming the cells, antibody, cytokines and phases.

Allergen → Th2 response → IL-4/IL-13 switch B cells to IgE (IL-5 activates eosinophils, IL-13 mucus) → IgE binds FcεRI on mast cells (sensitisation, silent) → re-exposure cross-links IgE → immediate phase in minutes with preformed histamine, proteases, chemokines (vasodilation, permeability, smooth-muscle spasm, mucus) → late phase over hours with newly made leukotrienes, PGD₂, PAF and cytokines recruiting eosinophils and neutrophils, causing sustained inflammation and tissue damage.

Why is a positive ANA insufficient to diagnose SLE?

ANA is almost always positive in SLE but not specific — it occurs in other autoimmune diseases, infections and healthy people, especially the elderly. Diagnosis needs 4 of 11 ACR criteria with at least one clinical and one immunological; the specific markers are anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm, with anti-C1q and complement levels tracking activity.

A patient develops burning and desquamation of the tongue two days after starting a new toothpaste. Mechanism, likely culprit, confirmation?

Oral contact allergy — type IV delayed hypersensitivity, consistent with 12–48 h onset. Likely a flavouring agent (cinnamon), often labelled only as "flavouring". Confirm by stop–restart; patch testing may support but not always confirm.

A patient collapses after you irrigate an extraction socket with chlorhexidine. What has happened and what do you do?

Anaphylaxis — a type I reaction to chlorhexidine entering an open vascular bed; fatalities are documented. Stop, call for help and an ambulance, give IM adrenaline 300 µg (autoinjector) into the lateral thigh, lie flat with legs raised, oxygen, repeat adrenaline every 5 minutes while symptoms persist, monitor and prepare for CPR.

Tutorial 5a — answer key

MCQ — hypersensitivity reactions are
c) Immune responses that cause tissue damage (incidental injury from a response aimed at foreign antigen).
MCQ — type III caused by deposition of
c) Immune complexes in tissues.
SAQ — definition and general causes
Incidental tissue injury from an immune response to foreign antigen. Causes: autoimmunity (SLE, Graves); microbes — excessive (TB granuloma), persistent, cross-reactive (rheumatic fever); environmental antigens in atopic individuals (pollen, peanut, latex).
SAQ — type I pathogenesis
Th2 → IL-4/13 (IgE switch), IL-5 (eosinophils); IgE on FcεRI; cross-linking; immediate phase (histamine, proteases) and late phase (leukotrienes, PGD₂, eosinophils).
SAQ — type II mechanisms + 2 diseases
Complement lysis/inflammation; opsonisation and phagocytosis/ADCC; receptor blockade or stimulation. Myasthenia gravis, Graves disease (or haemolytic anaemia, pemphigoid, transfusion reaction).
Scenario — bee-sting anaphylaxis
IgE cross-linking on mast cells → histamine, LTC4/D4, PGD₂, PAF → vasodilation and permeability (hypotension, angioedema, urticaria), bronchospasm and laryngeal oedema, GI cramps. First-line: IM adrenaline 300 µg, repeat 5-minutely, ambulance, supine/legs up, oxygen; antihistamine and steroid are adjuncts.
7

Chapter 7 · Tutorial 5b

Immunopathology 2 — Autoimmunity & Transplantation

Tolerance to self fails; tissue moves between people

Two topics with one thing in common: the immune system responding correctly to something it should have left alone. Autoimmunity borrows every effector mechanism from Chapter 6; transplantation shows what MHC is actually for.

Know these cold

  • Autoimmunity (a response) ≠ autoimmune disease (damage from it). A positive autoantibody is not a diagnosis
  • Genes load the gun — MHC alleles, apoptosis defects; environment pulls the trigger — infection (mimicry), hormones, drugs, UV
  • Female predominance except ankylosing spondylitis
  • Sjögren: CD4 T cells vs exocrine ducts; anti-SS-A (Ro), anti-SS-B (La); xerostomia
  • Hyperacute (preformed antibody, minutes) · acute (T cells, days–weeks, reversible) · chronic (fibrosis, years, not responsive)
  • Immunosuppression: infection (CMV, fungi) and 40× malignancy; GvHD reverses direction

Autoimmunity defined

AutoimmunityAn immune response against a self (auto-) antigen or antigens.
Autoimmune diseaseTissue damage or disturbed physiological function resulting from an autoimmune response.

The distinction is the examinable point: autoimmune responses can occur without disease. Low-affinity self-reactive B and T cells escape central deletion in everyone and are held in check by peripheral tolerance — anergy without co-stimulation, regulatory T cells, sequestration of antigen. Low-titre autoantibodies are common, rise with age and after infection, and cause nothing. Disease requires a response sustained and effective enough to injure tissue or disturb function — which needs genetic susceptibility plus a trigger. This is why a positive ANA alone cannot diagnose SLE.

Tutorial 5b MCQ 1: autoimmunity = b) immune response against self-antigens. SAQ 1: both definitions + how a response exists without disease.

Proving autoimmunity caused the disease

An association is not a cause. Four requirements, Koch's postulates applied to autoimmunity: demonstrate immunological reactivity to a self antigen; characterise or isolate the inciting autoantigen; induce reactivity in an experimental animal by immunising against the same antigen; show the same pathological changes in that animal's organs. (Passive transfer — disease following transfer of antibody or T cells, e.g. neonatal Graves and myasthenia from maternal IgG — is the clinical equivalent.)

Patterns

Organ-specificNon-organ-specific (systemic)
Single organ, commonly an endocrine gland; autoantibody against a cell-surface or intracellular molecule confined to that organ. Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, Addison, myasthenia gravis, pemphigus/pemphigoid, primary biliary cholangitis.Multiple organs, because the self antigen is widely distributed — particularly intracellular molecules involved in transcription and translation (DNA, histones, RNP, Sm). SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, Sjögren, dermatomyositis. SLE hits skin, joints, kidney, heart and blood because its target is in every nucleated cell.
Population affected~3% (5–8% with all autoimmune conditions)
Major chronic disabling examplesMultiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes
Peak onset15–65 years
SexAlmost all more common in women — except ankylosing spondylitis

Aetiology

Genetic factors

Usually polygenic; some single-gene defects involve apoptosis (Fas/FasL — ALPS; AIRE — APECED; FOXP3 — IPEX). The strongest and best characterised associations involve alleles of the MHC: HLA-B27 (ankylosing spondylitis, ~90×), DR3/DR4 (type 1 diabetes), DR4 (rheumatoid arthritis), DR2/DR3 (SLE), DQ2/DQ8 (coeliac). MHC determines which peptides are presented to T cells, so an allele that presents a self peptide well is a direct route to autoimmunity; apoptosis is how self-reactive lymphocytes are deleted, so a defect lets them survive. One controls what is shown; the other controls who may respond. SLE's numbers show polygenic susceptibility: >100 loci, 25% monozygotic concordance — three-quarters of identical twins are discordant, so something environmental pulls the trigger.

Environmental factors

FactorMechanism
HormonesFemale predominance; peak onset in reproductive years implicates oestrogen; ovariectomy inhibits onset in animal SLE models — the experimental evidence for causation.
InfectionMolecular mimicry — a microbial antigen resembles a self antigen so the response raised against one attacks the other (streptococcal M protein → rheumatic fever; Campylobacter → Guillain–Barré). Infection also up-regulates co-stimulatory molecules on APCs (bystander activation), alters antigen breakdown and presentation, and releases sequestered antigens through tissue damage.
DrugsA drug–self complex structurally resembles self and bypasses peripheral tolerance; some drugs bind directly in the MHC peptide groove and induce abnormal T-cell responses. HLA-DR2 — penicillamine-induced myasthenia; DR3 — nephritis. Slow acetylators are prone to drug-induced SLE (hydralazine, procainamide).
Ultraviolet radiationModifies self antigens (↑ immunogenicity) and causes apoptosis of keratinocytes; apoptosis externalises normally intracellular autoantigens onto the cell surface, where circulating autoantibodies can bind — the mechanism of lupus photosensitivity and flares.
Tutorial 5b SAQ 2: genetic (polygenic, MHC/HLA, apoptosis genes, twin concordance) + environmental (hormones, infection/mimicry, drugs, UV) → "genes load, environment triggers".

Mechanisms of tissue damage

Autoimmunity has no effector machinery of its own — it uses the hypersensitivity types of Chapter 6 with a self antigen.

RouteTypeExamples
Antibody against cell-bound antigenIIAutoimmune haemolytic anaemia, ITP, pemphigus/pemphigoid, Goodpasture; receptor interference — Graves (stimulating anti-TSHR), myasthenia (blocking anti-AChR)
Immune complexesIIISLE, rheumatoid vasculitis, some glomerulonephritides
CD4+ T cell-mediated — macrophage or CTL activationIVType 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, Hashimoto, rheumatoid synovitis, Sjögren
CombinationMixedMost real diseases — RA is III + IV; Sjögren is IV with diagnostic antibodies

Sjögren syndrome — the dental one

CD4+ T-cell reactions against unknown antigens in the ductal epithelium of exocrine glands — lacrimal and salivary — producing dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and xerostomia. Most patients with primary Sjögren have autoantibodies to the ribonucleoprotein antigens SS-A (Ro) and SS-B (La); ANA and rheumatoid factor are common. Primary (alone) vs secondary (with RA, SLE, scleroderma). Histology: periductal lymphocytic infiltrate, acinar atrophy, fibrosis — focus score on labial gland biopsy. Type IV damage with type II/III markers — the "combination" route. Dental consequences: rampant cervical and root caries, candidosis, angular cheilitis, burning mouth, dysphagia, difficulty with dentures, recurrent parotid swelling, and a ~5–10% lifetime risk of B-cell lymphoma (MALT). Management: saliva substitutes, sialogogues (pilocarpine), high fluoride, meticulous prevention, antifungals.

Treatment of autoimmune disease

Two options, neither a cure: replacement of organ function (thyroxine in Hashimoto, insulin in type 1 diabetes, B12 in pernicious anaemia, saliva substitutes in Sjögren) or immune suppression (corticosteroids, azathioprine, methotrexate, biologics such as anti-TNF and rituximab) — damping wanted immunity along with unwanted, with the same complications as transplant immunosuppression: infection and malignancy.

Transplantation — vocabulary

HaplotypeA group of genes inherited together from one parent.
AlleleA variant form of a gene.
AutograftFrom one part of one's own body to another (skin graft, bone graft from chin or hip) — no rejection.
Isograft / syngeneicBetween genetically identical individuals (identical twins).
AllograftBetween genetically dissimilar individuals of the same species — the usual clinical transplant.
XenograftAcross a species barrier (porcine valves, bovine bone substitute) — highest rejection risk.

MHC and HLA

Cell-surface glycoproteins of two basic types; in humans MHC antigens are the human leucocyte antigens (HLA), encoded on chromosome 6. Extensive polymorphism and co-dominant expression (each person expresses both parental haplotypes) are why matching unrelated people is so hard.

ClassGenesFound onPresents to
MHC IHLA-A, -B, -CMost nucleated cellsCD8+ cytotoxic T cells
MHC IIHLA-DP, -DQ, -DRAntigen-presenting cellsCD4+ helper T cells
MHC IIIC2, C4, factor B, TNFNot a presenting molecule — encodes complement components C2 and C4; grouped by chromosomal location, not function

How a graft is rejected

Afferent — initiation / sensitisationEffector
Allorecognition: donor MHC on donor dendritic cells (passenger leukocytes) is recognised by recipient CD4+ T cells — directly (donor MHC read as foreign) or indirectly (donor MHC peptides presented on recipient MHC). Occurs in the graft or in recipient lymphoid organs.CD4 cells enter the graft and recruit effectors with IL-2 and IFN-γ: macrophages, CD8 cytotoxic cells, NK cells, B cells/antibody. Targets: the endothelium and parenchymal cells.

Attacking the graft's endothelium destroys its blood supply, so rejection presents as infarction and progressive ischaemic failure — common to all three patterns.

RejectionTimingMechanismPathologyResponse to treatment
HyperacuteMinutes to hoursPre-formed circulating antibody against donor MHC class I or ABO (prior transfusion, pregnancy, transplant) → complement, endothelial injury, thrombosisCyanotic, mottled, flaccid graft; fibrin–platelet thrombi; neutrophils; necrosisNone — graft must be removed; prevented by ABO matching and cross-match
AcuteDays to weeks (up to months)T-cell (type IV) — CD8 infiltration and tubulitis/endothelialitis — ± antibody-mediated vasculitisInterstitial mononuclear infiltrate, oedema, endothelial damageReversible with immunosuppression (pulsed steroids, anti-T-cell agents)
ChronicMonths to yearsNot thought to be primarily immunological — intimal fibrosis and vascular obliteration (chronic allograft vasculopathy), ischaemia, repeated subclinical injury, drug toxicityInterstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy, glomerulosclerosis; slowly progressive failure with hypertensionSlowly progressive and not responsive to immunosuppression
Tutorial 5b MCQ 2: chronic rejection = c) slowly progressive, not responsive to immunosuppression. Pattern: antibody already there (minutes) → T cells primed (weeks, treatable) → fibrosis (years, untreatable).

Complications of immunosuppression

ComplicationDetail
InfectionViral — mainly CMV, also HSV, VZV, EBV, BK virus; opportunistic fungal — Cryptococcus, Candida, Aspergillus, Pneumocystis; bacterial and mycobacterial
Malignancy40× higher incidence — particularly Kaposi's sarcoma (HHV-8) and lymphoma (EBV); also skin SCC, lip cancer. Immune surveillance is invisible until removed
CardiovascularAcute MI from hypertension, hypertriglyceridaemia and steroid-aggravated insulin-resistant diabetes (ciclosporin, tacrolimus, steroids)
Drug-specificCiclosporin — gingival overgrowth, nephrotoxicity; steroids — osteoporosis, adrenal suppression, poor healing; azathioprine — marrow suppression

Dental implications: candidosis, herpetic and CMV ulceration, hairy leukoplakia, delayed healing after extraction, gingival overgrowth, oral Kaposi's sarcoma and lymphoma; consider antibiotic prophylaxis and steroid cover; screen the mouth for malignancy. The same applies to any patient immunosuppressed for autoimmune disease.

Bone marrow transplantation and GvHD

Haemopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) for leukaemia, lymphoma, aplastic anaemia, SCID. Complications: failure of engraftment, infection during aplasia, and graft-versus-host disease. In GvHD the transplanted immunocompetent cells recognise the recipient as foreign and attack — the direction of ordinary rejection reversed, because the graft is an immune system. Acute GvHD (first 100 days): skin rash, diarrhoea, jaundice. Chronic GvHD resembles systemic sclerosis and Sjögren.

Oral chronic GvHDFeatures
MucosaErythema, lichenoid lesions, ulceration, mucoceles
Salivary glandsHypofunction — dry mouth, caries, candidosis
SclerosisFibrosis with limited mouth opening

The dentist may be the first to recognise the triad, and mouth opening is easy to measure and track. HSCT patients also carry the infection and malignancy risks above, plus mucositis from conditioning chemotherapy.

Drill

SLE affects skin, joints, kidneys, heart and blood. What does that say about its target antigen?

That it is widely distributed — SLE is non-organ-specific. Its autoantigens are intracellular molecules of transcription and translation (nuclear antigens, dsDNA, Sm) present in every nucleated cell, so disease cannot be confined to one organ.

Why does sun exposure trigger a lupus flare?

UV causes keratinocyte apoptosis, and apoptosis externalises normally intracellular nuclear antigens onto the cell surface where circulating anti-nuclear antibodies bind, forming complexes that fix complement and damage tissue; UV also modifies self antigens, increasing immunogenicity. Defective clearance of apoptotic debris in SLE compounds this.

A kidney fails over several years despite full immunosuppression. Which rejection, and why doesn't treatment help?

Chronic rejection — months to years, slowly progressive failure with hypertension, intimal fibrosis and interstitial scarring. It is not primarily immunologically mediated, so immunosuppression has nothing to act on.

How does GvHD differ from ordinary rejection, and why does it occur in marrow transplants specifically?

Ordinary rejection: host attacks graft. GvHD: graft attacks host. It happens in HSCT because the transplanted tissue is an immune system whose donor T cells recognise recipient tissues as foreign — skin, gut, liver, and in the mouth lichenoid lesions, salivary hypofunction and sclerosis with limited opening.

Tutorial 5b — answer key

MCQ — autoimmunity is
b) An immune response against self-antigens.
MCQ — chronic rejection is
c) Slowly progressive and not responsive to immunosuppression.
SAQ — autoimmunity vs autoimmune disease; response without disease
Response against self antigen vs damage/dysfunction from it. Self-reactive clones exist in everyone, held by peripheral tolerance (anergy, Tregs, sequestration); low-titre autoantibodies are common and harmless; disease needs susceptibility + trigger. Hence ANA alone ≠ SLE.
SAQ — aetiological factors
Genetic: polygenic, HLA alleles (B27, DR3/DR4), apoptosis/tolerance genes (Fas, AIRE, FOXP3), 25% MZ concordance. Environmental: hormones (oestrogen, ovariectomy models), infection (molecular mimicry, bystander activation, antigen release), drugs (procainamide, hydralazine, penicillamine; slow acetylators), UV (apoptosis exposes nuclear antigen). Genes load, environment triggers; damage via types II, III, IV.

Chapter 8 · Tutorial 5c

Immunopathology 3 — Immunodeficiency

The primary defects, and the secondary immunodeficiency most likely to show first in the mouth

Parts 1 and 2 covered an immune system doing too much. This one covers it doing too little — and why the dentist, examining the tissue where opportunists first appear, is often the first to suspect it.

Know these cold

  • Immunodeficiency = defects in immune function; infections that are severe, persistent, unusual, recurrent
  • Primary = intrinsic (usually genetic, childhood) · secondary = consequence of another condition (HIV, drugs, malignancy)
  • Four primary arms: antibody, T cell, phagocyte, complement
  • CGD: NADPH oxidase absent → engulf but cannot kill → non-caseating granulomas
  • HIV: gp120–CD4 with CCR5/CXCR4; sexual transmission commonest; needlestick 0.3%
  • Oral four: erythematous candidosis, hairy leukoplakia, HSV, necrotising ulcerative periodontitis

Two categories

Primary immunodeficiencySecondary (acquired) immunodeficiency
CauseAn intrinsic defect in the immune system itself — usually genetic; typically presents in infancy or childhood (IgA deficiency and CVID may present later)Due to another underlying condition — infection (HIV), malignancy (lymphoma, leukaemia, myeloma), drugs (corticosteroids, cytotoxics, ciclosporin, biologics), malnutrition, diabetes, renal or liver failure, splenectomy, extremes of age, burns. Far more common
ExamplesX-linked agammaglobulinaemia, selective IgA deficiency, DiGeorge, SCID, chronic granulomatous disease, C1 esterase inhibitor and terminal complement deficienciesAIDS; the transplant patient of Chapter 7; the patient on long-term steroids or chemotherapy
PresentationInfections that are severe, persistent, unusual and recurrent; also failure to thrive, autoimmunity, and increased malignancy. Any one alone may mean nothing; together they say the immune system, not the organism, is the problem
Tutorial 5c MCQs 1–2: immune deficiency = b) defects in function; primary = b) intrinsic defect.

The four primary categories

Arm that failedExamplesOrganisms favoured
Antibody (B cell / humoral)X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinaemia, common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency (commonest — mucosal infection, atopy)Encapsulated bacteria — pneumococcus, Haemophilus; Giardia; enteroviruses
Cell-mediated (T cell)DiGeorge (thymic aplasia, 22q11), SCID (combined)Viruses (CMV, HSV), fungi (Candida, Pneumocystis), intracellular organisms; live vaccines dangerous
PhagocyteNeutropenia; chronic granulomatous disease; leukocyte adhesion deficiency; Chediak–HigashiStaphylococci, Gram-negatives, Aspergillus, Candida
ComplementC3 deficiency; terminal (C5–9) deficiency; C1 inhibitor deficiency (hereditary angioedema)Encapsulated bacteria; Neisseria with terminal defects; immune-complex disease/SLE with early-component defects

These are the four effector arms built in Chapter 4, each with its own failure mode. Knowing which arm has failed predicts which organisms cause trouble.

Primary defects in phagocyte function

The defect is neutropenia (too few — congenital, cyclic, or acquired from chemotherapy and marrow disease) or neutrophil dysfunction (enough, not working — CGD, adhesion or chemotaxis defects).

  1. Recurrent and persistent infectionsthe general marker.
  2. Severe infection but minimal clinical featuresthe clinical features of infection are the neutrophil response; without neutrophils there is little pus, redness or swelling. A neutropenic patient with a quiet-looking swelling may be critically ill.
  3. Poorly responsive to antibioticsantibiotics slow organisms; neutrophils remove them.
  4. Commonly staphylococcal; also Gram-negatives and fungi.
  5. Involve skin and mucous membranesthe barrier surfaces; oral ulceration, necrotising gingivitis, periodontal breakdown.
  6. Complicated by suppurative lymphadenopathy.

Chronic granulomatous disease

Failure to produce high concentrations of toxic oxygen radicals during the respiratory burst, because of a non-functional NADPH oxidase (X-linked or autosomal recessive). The phagocyte can find and engulf the organism but cannot kill it — catalase-positive organisms survive inside, and the immune system walls them off. Presents in the first 3 months of life with severe skin sepsis (Staphylococcus aureus) or fungal infection (Candida albicans, Aspergillus fumigatus). Complications: regional lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, hepatic abscesses, osteomyelitis, pneumonia. Organs show multiple abscesses and non-caseating giant-cell granulomas — persistent undestroyable organism = granuloma stimulus (Chapter 4), non-caseating unlike TB. Diagnosis: nitroblue tetrazolium or dihydrorhodamine test. Treatment: prophylactic antibiotics and antifungals, IFN-γ, HSCT.

HIV and AIDS

AIDS is caused by the retroviruses HIV-1 and HIV-2. Australia end-2015: 25,313 people living with HIV, 10% unaware of their status, 29% of new diagnoses made late — so a proportion of patients in the chair have undiagnosed HIV, the argument for standard precautions and for taking oral manifestations seriously.

Transmission

RouteDetail
Sexual intercourseThe dominant route worldwide — anal and vaginal; risk raised by ulcerative STIs, high viral load
Sharing contaminated needlesInjecting drug use; re-used therapeutic equipment
Receipt of infected materialBlood and blood products (now screened), donated organs, semen
Occupational exposureNeedle-stick or blood splash — 0.3% seroconversion per percutaneous exposure from a positive source (mucosal ~0.09%). Report every sharps injury; post-exposure prophylaxis within 72 h for 28 days
Vertical (mother-to-child)Before or during birth, or breastfeeding — almost all new childhood infections; reduced to <1% with ART

Not transmitted by saliva in dental practice, casual contact, or aerosol. Compare: hepatitis B needlestick ~30% (unvaccinated), hepatitis C ~3%, HIV 0.3%.

Tutorial 5c MCQ 3 / SAQ 2: most common mode = c) sexual intercourse. List all five routes.

Pathogenesis

  1. Entryenvelope glycoprotein gp120 binds CD4 (mainly helper T cells; also macrophages, dendritic cells, microglia), then a co-receptor — CCR5 (macrophage-tropic, early) or CXCR4 (T-tropic, late); gp41 mediates fusion. CCR5-Δ32 homozygotes are resistant.
  2. Reverse transcriptionviral RNA → DNA by reverse transcriptase (error-prone).
  3. Integrationproviral DNA inserted into the host genome by integrase; may lie latent in resting memory T cells (the reservoir that prevents cure).
  4. Replicationon T-cell activation: transcription, translation, assembly, protease cleavage, budding. 10⁹–10¹⁰ virions/day and up to 10⁸ new mutants/day.
  5. CD4 depletiondirect cytopathic lysis, apoptosis, syncytium formation, CTL killing of infected cells, chronic activation and exhaustion; lymphoid architecture destroyed. Count falls ~50–100 cells/µL/year.
  6. Consequencelosing the helper T cell disables the coordinator of every arm of immunity: B cells make poor antibody, macrophages are not activated, CTL responses fail → broad opportunistic infection and virally driven tumours.

Clinical spectrum — WHO stages

StageFeatures
1 — Acute seroconversion illnessTransient glandular-fever-like illness (fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, oral ulcers) in 10–20% within weeks of infection. Precedes seroconversion — the patient may be antibody-negative while highly infectious (window period; use p24/RNA tests)
2 — AsymptomaticClinical latency, years; virus replicating in lymphoid tissue; CD4 falling
3 — Persistent generalised lymphadenopathyEnlarged nodes at ≥2 extra-inguinal sites for ≥3 months
4 — AIDSCD4 typically <200/µL. AIDS-related complex: unexplained lymphadenopathy, diarrhoea, night sweats, oral candidiasis, weight loss. Neurological (HIV is neurotropic): at seroconversion aseptic meningitis, encephalopathy, myelopathy, neuropathy; later chronic meningitis, cerebral lymphoma, encephalopathy and dementia in up to 70%. Opportunistic infections and tumours below
Opportunistic infectionsTumours — both virally driven
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; CMV (retinitis, colitis, oral ulcers) and HSV; cerebral toxoplasmosis; cryptococcal meningitis; atypical mycobacteria (MAC) and TB; systemic fungal infection (candidosis, histoplasmosis); GI parasites (cryptosporidium)Kaposi's sarcoma — HHV-8 (purple macules → nodules on palate and gingiva; may be the presenting sign). Non-Hodgkin lymphoma — EBV (including cerebral and oral). Also cervical and anal carcinoma (HPV). Immune surveillance removed — the same two tumours as the 40× transplant figure

Oral manifestations — why the dentist is often first to know

CategoryLesionNotes
FungalErythematous (and pseudomembranous) candidosis, angular cheilitisRed sore mucosa without plaque is easily missed; unexplained candidosis in a young adult → think immunosuppression
Viral — EBVOral hairy leukoplakiaWhite, corrugated, bilateral lateral tongue, does not rub off; marker of immunosuppression; not premalignant; treatment not always needed
Viral — HSV / VZV / CMVHerpes simplex infection, zoster, CMV ulcersMore severe, persistent and extensive than in the immunocompetent; atypical sites
BacterialNecrotising ulcerative gingivitis / periodontitis, linear gingival erythemaRapid painful destruction with bone exposure, disproportionate to plaque
NeoplasticKaposi's sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphomaPalate and gingiva; purple macule → nodule; lymphoma as ulcerated swelling
OtherAphthous-like ulcers, HPV warts, salivary gland disease with xerostomia, parotid enlargement

The four to recognise: erythematous candidosis, hairy leukoplakia, herpes simplex, necrotising ulcerative periodontitis. Any of them in unexpectedly severe form in a young patient, or two together, warrants sensitive discussion and referral for testing. They are the opportunistic-infection categories — fungal, viral, viral, bacterial — presenting in the tissue you examine every day.

Tutorial 5c scenario: recurrent oral candidiasis + unexplained weight loss + persistent lymphadenopathy → HIV infection, stage 3 → 4 (AIDS-related complex). Pathogenesis steps: gp120–CD4/co-receptor entry → reverse transcription → integration/latency → replication with high mutation → CD4 depletion → loss of coordination → opportunistic infection.

Management

Treatment is combination antiretroviral therapy (ART / HAART) — suppression to undetectable viral load, immune recovery, and near-zero transmission (U=U); not a cure because of the latent proviral reservoir. Combination is essential because 10⁸ mutants/day make resistance to any single agent almost immediate; attacking several life-cycle steps at once means a virion would need several simultaneous mutations to escape.

ClassAction
Entry inhibitorsBind CCR5, blocking the co-receptor (maraviroc)
Fusion inhibitorsBlock gp41-mediated fusion of virus and cell membrane (enfuvirtide)
Reverse transcriptase inhibitorsNucleoside (tenofovir, emtricitabine, lamivudine) and non-nucleoside (efavirenz) — block replication
Integrase inhibitorsBlock integration of proviral DNA (dolutegravir) — backbone of current regimens
Protease inhibitorsPrevent cleavage and assembly of new virions (darunavir)

Why no vaccine: the envelope is fragile and a poor immunogen, and the mutation rate leaves no stable epitope. Prevention instead: condoms, needle exchange, screened blood, PrEP, PEP (within 72 h, 28 days), antenatal ART and safe feeding. Dental: standard precautions for all patients; well-controlled HIV on ART needs no treatment modification; check CD4 and viral load, neutrophil and platelet counts, drug interactions (protease inhibitors with midazolam, azoles), and manage the oral lesions above.

Drill

Why does a failure of NADPH oxidase produce granulomas?

NADPH oxidase generates the respiratory-burst oxygen radicals phagocytes use to kill ingested organisms. Without it organisms are engulfed but survive inside the cell; a persistent undestroyable organism is exactly the stimulus for granuloma formation, so the body walls it off — non-caseating giant-cell granulomas alongside multiple abscesses.

Why is HIV so devastating when it destroys only one cell type?

Because the CD4 helper T cell is the master regulator: it licenses B cells to make high-affinity antibody, activates macrophages via IFN-γ and supports CD8 responses. Removing it disables the coordination of every arm, producing a broad range of fungal, viral, protozoal and mycobacterial infections and virally driven tumours rather than one characteristic infection.

A young patient has severe necrotising ulcerative periodontitis and a white lateral-tongue lesion that does not rub off. What should you be thinking?

Both are recognised oral manifestations of HIV — NUP and oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV; not removable, unlike pseudomembranous candidosis). With 10% of HIV-positive people unaware and 29% diagnosed late, this combination in a young patient warrants sensitive discussion and referral for testing, while managing the periodontal disease.

Why is a negative HIV antibody test not reassuring in the weeks after a risk exposure?

The stage 1 seroconversion illness and peak viraemia precede antibody production; during this window the patient is antibody-negative but highly infectious. Repeat testing at the appropriate interval, or use p24 antigen / HIV RNA.

Tutorial 5c — answer key

MCQ — immune deficiency is characterised by
b) Defects in immune system function.
MCQ — primary immune deficiency is
b) An intrinsic defect in the immune system.
MCQ — most common HIV transmission
c) Sexual intercourse.
SAQ — define and distinguish primary vs secondary
Defects in immune function → severe/persistent/unusual/recurrent infection. Primary: intrinsic, usually genetic, childhood — XLA, IgA deficiency, DiGeorge, SCID, CGD, complement deficiency. Secondary: due to another condition — HIV, immunosuppressive drugs/steroids/chemo, malignancy, diabetes, malnutrition, splenectomy, age.
SAQ — HIV transmission routes
Sexual (most common), needle sharing, infected blood/products/organs, occupational needlestick (0.3%), vertical (perinatal, breastfeeding).
Scenario — candidiasis, weight loss, lymphadenopathy
HIV infection progressing toward AIDS-related complex. Pathogenesis: gp120–CD4 + CCR5/CXCR4 → RT → integration → replication/mutation → CD4 depletion → loss of helper coordination → opportunistic infection (Candida) and lymphadenopathy; confirm with serology/RNA, CD4 count, viral load.
