Chapter 9 · Tutorial 7A

Neoplasia 1 — Nomenclature & Features

What makes a growth a neoplasm, what makes a neoplasm malignant, and how it harms the patient

Every adaptation in Chapter 2 regresses when its stimulus is removed. A neoplasm does not — it has become autonomous. This chapter fixes the vocabulary, the benign-versus-malignant criteria, and the effects a tumour has on the person carrying it.

Know these cold

  • Neoplasm = abnormal growth of cells that persists in the absence of the initiating stimulus
  • Invasion and metastasis are the only absolute discriminators of malignancy
  • Malignant cytology: frequent/atypical mitoses, anaplasia, pleomorphism, hyperchromatism, ↑ N:C ratio
  • -oma benign; carcinoma = epithelial; sarcoma = mesenchymal; adenoma/adenocarcinoma = glandular
  • Malignant despite -oma: lymphoma, melanoma, mesothelioma, seminoma
  • Anaplasia = lack of differentiation; a reliable indicator of malignancy
  • Dysplasia: drop-shaped rete ridges, superficial mitoses; benign harm = pressure, obstruction, hormone, transformation, anxiety

Tumour and neoplasm

Tumour has two meanings — an abnormal swelling, or a neoplasm — so it is loose: an abscess or a haematoma is a swelling too. A neoplasm is a lesion resulting from the autonomous or relatively autonomous abnormal growth of cells that persists in the absence of the initiating stimulus. The phrase that carries the definition is "persists in the absence of the initiating stimulus": hypertrophy, hyperplasia and metaplasia (Chapter 2) all regress when the stimulus is removed; a neoplasm does not. Every neoplasm is a tumour; not every tumour is a neoplasm.

Tutorial 7A MCQ 1: neoplasm = d) abnormal growth that persists in the absence of the initiating stimulus.

A neoplasm has two components: the parenchyma — the transformed, neoplastic cells, the tumour proper — and the stroma — host-derived supporting connective tissue, the route by which the tumour gets its blood supply (and later, its angiogenesis, Chapter 10).

Benign and malignant

Benign: microscopic and gross characteristics are relatively innocent, implying the lesion will remain localised and is amenable to local surgical removal. Malignant: the lesion can invade and destroy adjacent structures and spread to distant sites (metastasise) to cause death.

FeatureBenignMalignant
Growth rateSlowRelatively rapid
MitosesInfrequent, normalFrequent and atypical (tripolar, asymmetric)
Resemblance to normal tissue (differentiation)GoodVariable, often poor — anaplasia
Nuclear morphologyNear normalEnlarged, hyperchromatic, irregular outline, multiple/prominent nucleoli, pleomorphic (variable size and shape); high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio
BorderCircumscribed, often encapsulated (compressed surrounding tissue)Poorly defined, infiltrative
Growth on a surfaceOften exophytic — piles up outward; pedunculated or sessileOften endophytic — burrows in; ulcerated, indurated, rolled everted margin, fixed
Necrosis / haemorrhageRareCommon — outgrows supply; bleeds from ulcerated surfaces
InvasionNoYes — breaches basement membrane, infiltrates stroma, perineural and vascular spaces
MetastasisNoYes — lymphatic (carcinomas), haematogenous (sarcomas), transcoelomic

Invasion and metastasis are the only absolute discriminators. Everything else — growth rate, mitoses, nuclear appearance — is a tendency with exceptions. A slow-growing, well-differentiated lesion that invades is still malignant. Clinically, an ulcerated, indurated lesion with rolled margins worries you more than a pedunculated lump.

Tutorial 7A MCQ 3: malignant = b) frequent mitoses and anaplasia. MCQ 4: anaplasia = b) decreased differentiation.

Nomenclature

Names encode tissue of origin (root) and behaviour (suffix). Learn the root and the suffix separately and most names decode themselves — apart from four exceptions.

Tissue of originBenignMalignant
Squamous epitheliumSquamous papillomaSquamous cell carcinoma — by far the commonest oral malignancy
Glandular / ductal epitheliumAdenoma (cystadenoma if cystic)Adenocarcinoma — grows in a glandular pattern (thyroid, colon, salivary)
Transitional epitheliumTransitional cell papillomaTransitional (urothelial) carcinoma
Fibrous tissueFibromaFibrosarcoma
FatLipomaLiposarcoma
CartilageChondromaChondrosarcoma
BoneOsteomaOsteosarcoma
Smooth / skeletal muscleLeiomyoma / rhabdomyomaLeiomyosarcoma / rhabdomyosarcoma
Blood vesselsHaemangiomaAngiosarcoma (Kaposi's sarcoma)
MelanocytesNaevusMelanoma
Lymphoid / haemopoietic—Lymphoma, leukaemia, myeloma
OdontogenicAmeloblastoma (benign but locally aggressive), odontomaAmeloblastic carcinoma (rare)
TermMeaning
-omaBenign neoplasm (fibroma, chondroma, adenoma)
CarcinomaMalignant neoplasm of epithelial cells, regardless of tissue of origin
AdenocarcinomaMalignant neoplasm of glandular or ductal epithelium growing in a glandular pattern
SarcomaMalignant neoplasm of solid mesenchymal (connective) tissue
-blastomaEmbryonal tumour (retinoblastoma, neuroblastoma)
TeratomaGerm-cell tumour with derivatives of more than one germ layer
Hamartoma / choristomaDisorganised but mature native tissue / normal tissue in an abnormal site — not true neoplasms
-oma but malignant: lymphoma, melanoma, mesothelioma, seminoma (add leukaemia, hepatoma, glioma). "Malignant melanoma" is redundant; the benign counterpart is a naevus. Tutorial 7A MCQ 2: benign glandular = c) adenoma.

Differentiation, anaplasia and dysplasia

Differentiation is the extent to which a neoplasm resembles its parenchymal cells of origin, morphologically and functionally. Well-differentiated tumours keep the architecture and products of the parent tissue (keratin pearls in SCC, hormone secretion in an adenoma). Anaplasia is lack of differentiation; tumours of undifferentiated cells are anaplastic, a reliable indicator of malignancy. Good differentiation does not exclude malignancy; anaplasia essentially confirms it. Grading (well / moderately / poorly differentiated) is based on it.

Dysplasia sits between: disordered but not yet malignant growth, with architectural and cellular atypia confined by the basement membrane. Carcinoma in situ = full-thickness dysplasia without invasion.

Oral epithelial dysplasia — sixteen features

Architectural (organisation of the epithelium)Cellular (individual cells)
Irregular epithelial maturation · loss of polarity of basal cells · drop-shaped rete ridges · increased mitotic figures · abnormally superficial mitotic figures · premature keratinisation in single cells · keratin pearls within rete ridges · loss of epithelial cell cohesionAbnormal variation in nuclear size and shape · abnormal variation in cell size and shape · increased nuclear–cytoplasmic ratio · atypical mitotic figures · increased number and size of nucleoli · nuclear hyperchromatism

Mitosis is normally confined to the basal layer, with cells maturing and losing the ability to divide as they move up; a mitotic figure high in the epithelium means maturation control has been lost. Graded mild (lower third), moderate (to middle third), severe (upper third) — the "degree of dysplasia" that Chapter 6 of L6 correlated with candidal carriage, and what the pathologist is counting in a biopsied leukoplakia.

Clinical effects of neoplasms

Benign — harm by position and functionMalignant — all of those, plus invasion
Pressure on adjacent tissue — a benign meningeal tumour causing epilepsy · obstruction of flow — a benign epithelial tumour blocking a duct (salivary), airway, bowel · hormone production — a thyroid adenoma causing thyrotoxicosis, a pituitary adenoma · transformation into a malignant neoplasm — adenomatous polyp → adenocarcinoma · anxiety — the patient fears something sinister, a reason to investigate promptly · also haemorrhage, infection, torsionPressure on and destruction of adjacent tissue · metastases — the defining effect · blood loss from ulcerated surfaces (anaemia) · obstruction — colonic tumour causing intestinal obstruction · hormone production — ACTH and ADH from lung tumours · other paraneoplastic effects — weight loss, debility · anxiety and pain · nerve involvement (paraesthesia of the lip in a mandibular malignancy)

"Benign" does not mean harmless — location and secretion matter as much as behaviour, which is why benign lesions in confined spaces (skull, duct, airway) are treated seriously.

Cachexia and paraneoplastic syndromes

Cancer cachexia: progressive loss of body fat and lean body mass with profound weakness, anorexia and anaemia — driven by cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-6) and raised metabolic rate, not simply by the tumour's consumption. A paraneoplastic syndrome is a symptom complex in a cancer patient that cannot be explained by local or distant spread, or by hormones indigenous to the tissue of origin. Commonest: hypercalcaemia (PTHrP from squamous carcinomas), Cushing syndrome (ectopic ACTH from small-cell lung cancer), non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (hypercoagulability); also SIADH, myasthenic syndromes, dermatomyositis, clubbing. They matter because they may be the earliest manifestation of an occult neoplasm, may be lethal in themselves, and may mimic metastatic disease and confound treatment. A lung tumour making ADH qualifies (lung does not make ADH); a thyroid tumour making thyroxine does not.

Epidemiology

The lecture presents worldwide age-standardised incidence and mortality, age-specific rates by sex, five-year survival trends (1984–88 to 2009–13), the top ten cancer sites worldwide and the most common Australian cancers. Take from the graphs: incidence and mortality maps differ — high-income regions record more incidence, lower-income regions have a worse mortality-to-incidence ratio (detection and treatment access, not just biology); incidence rises steeply with age, consistent with the multistep accumulation of mutations; and five-year survival has improved substantially. Lip, oral cavity and pharyngeal cancers do not top the lists but are cancers a dentist is uniquely placed to detect early.

Carcinogens and host factors

Classes of carcinogenHost factors
Chemicals (tobacco PAHs and nitrosamines, alcohol/acetaldehyde, aromatic amines, asbestos) · viruses (HPV, EBV, HHV-8, HBV/HCV) · ionising and non-ionising radiation (X-rays, UV) · exogenous hormones (oestrogens) · microbial agents (H. pylori, chronic candidal inflammation)Race · diet · constitutional factors (sex, age, inherited risk — BRCA, retinoblastoma, familial polyposis) · premalignant lesions and conditions (leukoplakia, erythroplakia, oral submucous fibrosis, lichen planus, chronic hyperplastic candidosis, syphilitic leukoplakia, actinic cheilitis) · transplacental exposure · immunosuppression · P450 polymorphisms and DNA-repair capacity

Carcinogenesis needs both columns: the same exposure produces cancer in one person and not another. The carcinogen supplies the insult; the host determines how it is metabolised, how well the damage is repaired, and whether a transformed cell survives immune surveillance.

Drill

Define neoplasia and give three microscopic and three macroscopic features distinguishing benign from malignant.

A neoplasm is an abnormal, autonomous growth of cells that persists in the absence of the initiating stimulus. Microscopic: mitoses (few and normal vs frequent and atypical); differentiation (good vs variable to anaplastic); nuclei (normal vs enlarged, hyperchromatic, pleomorphic, high N:C ratio with prominent nucleoli). Macroscopic: border (circumscribed/encapsulated vs poorly defined, infiltrative); surface growth (exophytic vs endophytic, ulcerated, indurated); necrosis and haemorrhage (rare vs common). Absolute discriminators: invasion and metastasis.

Describe tumour nomenclature with examples of each category.

Benign: tissue root + -oma — lipoma, chondroma, adenoma, squamous papilloma, haemangioma, leiomyoma. Malignant epithelial: carcinoma — squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma (glandular), basal cell carcinoma. Malignant mesenchymal: sarcoma — liposarcoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma. Exceptions ending in -oma but malignant: lymphoma, melanoma, mesothelioma, seminoma. Embryonal: -blastoma.

Why can a paraneoplastic syndrome complicate treatment rather than just accompany it?

Because it may mimic metastatic disease — hypercalcaemia or unexplained systemic illness can suggest widespread spread and push management toward palliation when the primary is still curable. It may also be the first sign of an occult tumour, and may itself be lethal.

A pedunculated pink lump on the gingiva vs an indurated ulcer with rolled margins on the lateral tongue. Which features push each toward benign or malignant, and what do you do?

The pedunculated exophytic lump with a defined border is the benign growth pattern (fibroma, papilloma, pyogenic granuloma). The endophytic, indurated, rolled-margin ulcer is the malignant pattern — likely SCC. Induration means infiltration into stroma. Both need a diagnosis, but the tongue lesion needs urgent biopsy and neck examination; a persistent lesion of more than 2–3 weeks is biopsied regardless of appearance.

MCQ — malignant neoplasms are characterised by

Definition (autonomous, persists without stimulus). Micro: mitoses, differentiation/anaplasia, nuclear pleomorphism/hyperchromatism/N:C. Macro: border/capsule, exophytic vs endophytic/ulcerated/indurated, necrosis/haemorrhage; invasion and metastasis absolute.

Chapter 10 · Tutorial 7B

Neoplasia 2 — Pathogenesis & Hallmarks

How a cell becomes autonomous: genes, epigenetics, the eight hallmarks and viral shortcuts

Chapter 9 described what a neoplasm looks like; this chapter explains how it comes to exist. Cancer is a disease of accumulated genetic and epigenetic change in a single cell lineage, and Hanahan and Weinberg's hallmarks are the framework that organises every mechanism.

Know these cold

  • Tumourigenesis = neoplastic transformation driven by genetic and epigenetic alterations; malignant transformation adds invasion and metastasis
  • Initiation (carcinogen induces mutation) → promotion (clonal proliferation) → progression (malignant behaviour)
  • Tumour suppressors need two hits (recessive); oncogenes need one (dominant) — p53 dominant-negative is the exception
  • p53 (17p): G1 arrest and repair, or apoptosis; mutated in >70% of cancers. RB gates G1/S
  • Eight hallmarks + two enablers (genomic instability, tumour-promoting inflammation)
  • No tumour exceeds 1–2 mm without angiogenesis
  • HPV E6 → p53, E7 → pRb — Hallmark 2 acquired by infection, not mutation

Neoplastic transformation

Neoplastic transformation (tumourigenesis) is the process by which a normal cell acquires the genetic and epigenetic alterations that make its growth autonomous — a single cell gains a survival and proliferation advantage and founds a clone. Two kinds of change:

Genetic alterationsEpigenetic changes
Point mutations (nonsense, missense), deletions, insertions, translocations (BCR-ABL, MYC–IgH), rearrangements, amplifications (HER2, MYC), aneuploidy. The sequence is changed — permanent and heritable through division.Promoter methylation silencing transcription, histone modification, microRNA dysregulation. The DNA sequence is unchanged but the gene is switched off or on — reversible in principle, invisible to sequencing.

Malignant transformation is the further acquisition of invasion and metastasis. Neoplastic transformation makes a cell autonomous; malignant transformation adds spread. A benign neoplasm has undergone the first without the second — which is why some benign lesions later progress, as an adenomatous polyp does to adenocarcinoma.

Tutorial 7B MCQ 1: tumourigenesis is primarily driven by b) genetic and epigenetic alterations.

Initiation, promotion, progression

  1. InitiationA carcinogen induces the genetic alteration(s) that give the transformed cell its neoplastic potential — irreversible but silent; the initiated cell looks normal. Chemical (tobacco PAHs → DNA adducts), radiation (UV dimers, X-ray breaks), viral (integration).
  2. PromotionStimulation of clonal proliferation of the initiated cell — promoters are not themselves mutagenic (hormones, chronic inflammation, alcohol, repeated irritation, phorbol esters); the effect is reversible and requires repeated, prolonged exposure; proliferation fixes the mutation and exposes the clone to further hits.
  3. ProgressionThe process culminating in malignant behaviour — further mutations, genomic instability, heterogeneity, selection of aggressive subclones, invasion, metastasis, drug resistance. Benign → malignant (adenoma → carcinoma).
ClonalOriginating from a single cell transformed by cumulative mutational events — every cell in the tumour inherits the founder's alterations, which is what makes molecular markers and targeted therapy possible
PolyclonalOriginating from multiple cells (hyperplasia, reactive lesions)
CarcinogenAn environmental agent participating in the causation of tumours
Multistep carcinogenesisThe hypothesis that cancer requires an accumulation of several successive changes, not one — explaining latency, age-dependence and the adenoma–carcinoma sequence
Tutorial 7B MCQ 2: initiation = c) induction of genetic alterations by a carcinogen.

Three genetic routes to a transformed cell

RouteWhat happensGenetics
Oncogene activationActivation or abnormal expression of oncogenes — an accelerator stuck onOne activated allele is enough — dominant at cell level (gain of function)
Loss of a tumour suppressorLoss or inactivation of both copies — a brake removedBoth copies must be lost — recessive at cell level, the double-hit model (loss of function)
Expression of telomeraseRestores the ability to divide indefinitely (Hallmark 5)Re-expression of a normally silent enzyme

Brakes must both fail; one stuck accelerator is enough. Add the genes of apoptosis (BCL2 up, BAX down) and DNA repair (genomic instability) as the supporting cast.

Tumour suppressor genes

The double-hit model: the first hit is the acquired mutational loss, or inheritance of a defective allele, of a tumour suppressor gene — the other, wild-type allele still expresses sufficient suppressive effect. The second hit is acquired loss of the normal allele, fully depriving the cell of suppression. Someone born with one defective allele carries the first hit in every cell and needs only one further event in any single cell — which is why familial cancers present earlier, bilaterally and multifocally (retinoblastoma, familial adenomatous polyposis/APC, BRCA1/2, Li–Fraumeni/TP53, NF1).

Caretaker genesGatekeeper genes
Maintain the integrity of the genome by repairing DNA damage — mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2), BRCA1/2, ATM, XP genes. Lose them and mutations accumulate.Inhibit proliferation or promote death of cells with damaged DNA — RB, p53, p16, APC, PTEN. Lose them and mutated cells are permitted to divide.
Tutorial 7B MCQ 3: the double-hit model is most relevant to c) tumour suppressor gene inactivation.

p53 — guardian of the genome

On the short arm of chromosome 17; the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer — defective in more than 70% of cancers, with the remainder often having defects upstream or downstream. Normally it senses DNA damage and (1) arrests the cycle in G1 (via p21) until damage is repaired before S phase, (2) drives senescence, or (3) induces apoptosis (via BAX, PUMA) if damage is extensive. Loss lets DNA-damaged cells survive and replicate (Chapter 2).

Mechanism of p53 lossDetail
MutationNonsense (unreadable) or missense (defective or altered-function protein); Li–Fraumeni syndrome inherits one mutant allele
Dominant-negative complexesMutant p53 forms complexes with normal p53 in heterozygous cells and inactivates or subverts it — one mutated allele can suffice; the explicit exception to the two-hit model
Viral protein bindingNormal p53 bound and degraded by proteins of oncogenic DNA viruses — HPV E6, polyomaviruses; the gene is normal, the protein is neutralised
MDM2 amplificationExcess of the protein that degrades p53

Genomic instability

Cells that have lost the mechanisms for sensing and repairing DNA damage have genomic instability — an enabling characteristic that accelerates accumulation of the mutations that actually drive growth. Chromosomal instability (breaks — Fanconi anaemia, ataxia telangiectasia); microsatellite instability from defective mismatch repair (HNPCC/Lynch syndrome — familial carcinoma of caecum and proximal colon, also endometrium); xeroderma pigmentosum — autosomal recessive nucleotide-excision repair defect, greatly increased cancer in sun-exposed skin.

Oncogenes

Oncogenes are genes driving the neoplastic behaviour of cells, derived from normal proto-oncogenes by gain of function. Two routes to activation: an altered protein that is excessively active (point mutation — RAS), or too much normal protein (amplification — HER2, MYC; translocation to an active promoter — BCR-ABL, MYC–IgH in Burkitt; viral insertion). Detected as more oncoprotein, more mRNA, or increased gene copy number.

Class (following the signalling pathway)Example oncogeneProduct / cancer
Growth factorssisPDGF β-chain — astrocytoma, osteosarcoma
Growth-factor receptorserbB1/2 (EGFR, HER2), RETLung, head-and-neck SCC; breast; MEN2
Membrane tyrosine kinasesrc, ABLBCR-ABL in CML — target of imatinib
Signal transducer (GTP-binding)RAS (K-, H-, N-)Commonest oncogene mutation — colon, pancreas, lung; locked GTP-bound "on"
Nuclear transcription factorsMYC, JUN, FOSBurkitt lymphoma (t(8;14)), neuroblastoma (N-MYC amplification)
Cell-cycle regulatorsCyclin D, CDK4Mantle-cell lymphoma, melanoma
Anti-apoptoticBCL2Follicular lymphoma (t(14;18))

Normal proliferation, which oncogenes hijack at any step: growth factor binds its receptor → transient and limited receptor activation → signal-transducing proteins on the inner membrane → transmission across the cytosol → nuclear regulatory factors initiate transcription and biosynthesis → cell-cycle entry. Cancer converts "transient" into continuous — which is Hallmark 1.

Epigenetic contributions

MechanismEffect
Promoter hypermethylationSilencing of tumour suppressors by methylation of CpG islands (p16, MLH1, BRCA1) — intact but unread; as unprotected as if deleted, invisible to sequencing, and reversible (demethylating drugs)
Histone modificationMethylation, acetylation, phosphorylation — the "histone code" opening or closing chromatin (HDAC inhibitors)
microRNAShort inhibitory RNA: more miRNA degrades mRNA and reduces expression (oncomiRs silencing suppressors); less miRNA enhances expression of oncogenes
Copy-number changeTo enhancer and regulatory regions

The hallmarks of cancer

Hanahan and Weinberg (2000, 2011): the acquired capabilities that every cancer must gain, however it gets them, plus two enabling characteristics that make acquiring them easier.

#HallmarkIn one lineMechanism
1Self-sufficiency in growth signalsMakes its own acceleratorGain-of-function oncogenes: own growth factors or stromal induction; overexpressed/mutant receptors; downstream RAS/RAF/PI3K; continuous MYC; CDK4/cyclin D gain, CDKI loss
2Insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signalsIgnores the brakesLoss of RB (G1/S gate), TP53, p16, TGF-β pathway, APC; loss of contact inhibition (Chapter 5)
3Altered cellular metabolismRefuels for buildingWarburg effect — aerobic glycolysis to lactate despite oxygen, supplying carbon skeletons for synthesis; a consequence of the same deregulated signalling as 1 and 2 (basis of PET-FDG imaging)
4Evasion of cell deathRefuses to dieBCL2 up, BAX/PUMA down, p53 out; disabled intrinsic pathway; CD95/Fas down
5Unlimited replicative potentialNever ages outTelomerase re-expression avoids senescence and mitotic catastrophe (~90% of cancers)
6Sustained angiogenesisBuilds its own supply linesNo solid tumour can exceed 1–2 mm without inducing angiogenesis — balance tipped to promoters (VEGF, FGF, hypoxia/HIF-1) over inhibitors (thrombospondin); uses the wound-healing machinery of Chapter 5; anti-VEGF drugs
7Invasion and metastasisLeaves homeLoosening (E-cadherin loss) → matrix degradation (MMPs) → migration → intravasation → survival in circulation → extravasation → colonisation. Site set by anatomy/vascular drainage (colon → liver) and tropism (prostate → bone). The major cause of morbidity and death
8Evasion of immune surveillanceHides from the immune systemAntigenic yet tolerated: loss of MHC I, immunosuppressive cytokines (TGF-β), regulatory T cells, and checkpoint ligands — PD-L1 on tumour cells switching off T cells; checkpoint-blocking antibodies (anti-PD-1/PD-L1, anti-CTLA-4) release the brake
+Genomic instabilityEnablerMutation accumulates faster — HNPCC, XP, p53 loss
+Tumour-promoting inflammationEnablerInflammatory cells supply growth factors, remove growth suppressors, resist death, drive angiogenesis, invasion and immune evasion — six of the eight hallmarks from outside the tumour cell; why chronic inflammation is a cancer risk
Tutorial 7B MCQ 4 (angiogenesis): c) it provides tumours with a nutrient and oxygen supply beyond a certain size.

Hallmarks 1 and 2 in the cell cycle

Two main checkpoints — G1/S and G2/M — each balanced by growth-promoting and growth-suppressing factors and by DNA-damage sensors. RB is the key negative regulator of the G1/S checkpoint, the portal through which cells must pass before DNA replication: hypophosphorylated RB binds and silences the transcription factor E2F; growth signals raise cyclin D–CDK4/6, which phosphorylate RB, release E2F and commit the cell to S phase; growth inhibitors (TGF-β, p16, contact inhibition) act by keeping RB active. At least one of p16, cyclin D, CDK4 or RB is mutated in most human cancers. p53-mediated arrest is the primordial response to DNA damage, acting through the same gate (p21 inhibits CDKs, keeping RB active).

Tutorial 7B scenario — RB1 mutation. Loss of RB frees E2F permanently: the cell enters S phase without needing external growth factors (Hallmark 1) and cannot respond to TGF-β, p16 or contact inhibition, all of which act through RB (Hallmark 2). Additional cell-cycle mutations (cyclin D/CDK4 gain, p16 or p53 loss) reinforce both and disable the damage checkpoint, so further mutations accumulate.

Targeted therapy follows from the framework: knowing which hallmark a tumour has acquired and how lets treatment aim at a receptor (trastuzumab), a kinase (imatinib), a vessel (bevacizumab) or an immune checkpoint, rather than at dividing cells in general as cytotoxic chemotherapy does.

Viral carcinogenesis

Virus typeMechanismExamples
Oncogenic DNA virusViral DNA integrates into host DNA; viral oncogenes are expressed — HPV E6 binds and degrades p53, E7 binds and inactivates pRb — disabling both gatekeepers without mutating either geneHPV-16/18 (cervical, oropharyngeal), EBV (Burkitt and other lymphomas, nasopharyngeal ca, hairy leukoplakia), HHV-8 (Kaposi's), HBV, Merkel-cell polyomavirus
"Acute" transforming RNA retrovirusRetroviral RNA has picked up a transcribed copy of a cellular oncogene from a prior host; reverse transcribed and integrated, the viral genome now carries a viral oncogene (v-src, v-ras) — brings its own acceleratorRous sarcoma virus (animal)
"Slow" transforming RNA retrovirusCarries no oncogene; inserts its promoter/enhancer next to a cellular oncogene and over-expresses it — stands on the accelerator you already hadFeline leukaemia virus; HTLV-1 (adult T-cell leukaemia)

Squamous papilloma — HPV-6/11 — is the benign end of the same spectrum: an exophytic, pedunculated, cauliflower-like lesion, not premalignant, treated by conservative excision. High-risk HPV-16 in the oropharynx (tonsil, base of tongue, presenting as a neck node) is the malignant end, the only oral-region carcinogen with a vaccine.

Drill

Why does a tumour suppressor need both copies lost, but an oncogene only one activated allele?

A suppressor is a brake: one functioning allele still makes enough protein to hold the cell, so both must be lost — recessive at the cellular level, the double-hit model. An oncogene is an accelerator: one constitutively active allele makes an always-on protein whose signal the normal allele cannot cancel — dominant. Exception on the suppressor side: dominant-negative mutant p53 poisons the normal protein, so one hit can suffice.

Define tumourigenesis and explain how genetic and epigenetic alterations contribute.

Neoplastic transformation is the acquisition, in a single cell lineage, of heritable alterations that make growth autonomous. Genetic alterations change the sequence — activating oncogenes (RAS point mutation, MYC amplification, BCR-ABL translocation) or inactivating tumour suppressors (RB, TP53 deletion/mutation) — and are fixed by clonal proliferation. Epigenetic alterations change expression without changing sequence — promoter hypermethylation silencing p16 or MLH1, histone modification, miRNA dysregulation — with the same functional effect, reversible and invisible to sequencing. Together they satisfy the hallmarks through the multistep sequence of initiation, promotion and progression.

A solid tumour has every mutation needed for malignancy but stays at 2 mm. What is missing?

Angiogenesis. Beyond 1–2 mm diffusion cannot supply oxygen and nutrients to the centre; growth resumes only when the balance of promoters (VEGF, FGF, driven by hypoxia) over inhibitors is tipped and new vessels are recruited from the stroma.

How does an oncogenic DNA virus cause cancer without mutating any host gene?

Its genome integrates and expresses viral oncogenes whose products bind the host's tumour-suppressor proteins: HPV E6 inactivates p53 and E7 inactivates pRb. The host genes are structurally normal; their proteins are neutralised, so the G1/S gate and the DNA-damage response are both lost — Hallmark 2 by infection.

Tutorial 7B — answer key

MCQ — tumourigenesis is primarily driven by
b) Genetic and epigenetic alterations.
MCQ — initiation phase involves
c) Induction of genetic alterations by a carcinogen.
MCQ — double-hit model is most relevant to
c) Tumour suppressor gene inactivation.
MCQ — role of angiogenesis
c) Provides a nutrient and oxygen supply beyond a certain size (1–2 mm).
SAQ — define tumourigenesis; genetic and epigenetic contributions
Acquisition of heritable alterations conferring autonomous growth in one clone. Genetic: oncogene gain of function (mutation, amplification, translocation), suppressor loss (two hits), telomerase, repair-gene loss. Epigenetic: promoter hypermethylation, histone code, miRNA — expression changed without sequence change; reversible.
SAQ — three phases of multistep carcinogenesis
Initiation: carcinogen induces irreversible mutation in a cell. Promotion: non-mutagenic promoter stimulates clonal proliferation of the initiated cell; reversible, needs repeated exposure. Progression: further mutations/genomic instability → heterogeneity, invasion, metastasis — malignant behaviour.
Scenario — RB1 mutation and Hallmarks 1 & 2
RB gates G1/S by binding E2F. Loss releases E2F permanently: S-phase entry without growth factors (self-sufficiency) and no response to TGF-β, p16, contact inhibition which act through RB (insensitivity to inhibition). Other cell-cycle mutations (cyclin D/CDK4 gain, p16/p53 loss) compound both and disable damage arrest.

Threads that run through all ten chapters

Cell type decides the outcomeCh 2 labile/stable/permanent → Ch 3 resolution vs repair → Ch 5 healing vs organisation. Oral mucosa regenerates; nerve and cardiac muscle scar; bone is the exception that regenerates as bone.
The agent you cannot removeCh 3 stop condition → Ch 4 chronic inflammation and granuloma → periodontitis (plaque), TB (mycobacterium), sutures and implants (frustrated phagocytosis), atherosclerosis (oxidised LDL), CGD (defective killing, Ch 8).
Apoptosis is silentCh 2 membrane intact → Ch 3 neutrophils die by apoptosis so inflammation ends → Ch 7 apoptosis deletes self-reactive lymphocytes; when it fails, autoimmunity; UV-induced apoptosis exposes nuclear antigen in SLE.

The macrophage–T cell loopCh 4 lymphokines and monokines → Ch 6 type IV (Th1 IFN-γ activating macrophages) → granuloma in TB, sarcoid, CGD; acute transplant rejection (Ch 7).
Immune surveillanceCh 4 NK cells and MHC I → Ch 7 40× malignancy on immunosuppression → Ch 8 Kaposi's sarcoma (HHV-8) and lymphoma (EBV) in HIV → Ch 10 Hallmark 8, PD-L1 and checkpoint blockade — the tumour achieving locally what immunosuppression does systemically.
Adaptation → dysplasia → neoplasiaCh 2 metaplasia (Barrett's) regresses when the stimulus stops; Ch 5 contact inhibition is the brake on regeneration; Ch 9 a neoplasm persists without the stimulus and dysplasia is the step between; Ch 10 loss of RB/contact inhibition is Hallmark 2.
Inflammation feeds tumoursCh 4 the macrophage's growth factors and angiogenic factors → Ch 5 VEGF and granulation tissue → Ch 10 tumour-promoting inflammation supplies six of eight hallmarks and angiogenesis is the 1–2 mm size limit.

Molecular mimicryCh 6 rheumatic heart disease as cross-reactivity → Ch 7 infection as an environmental cause of autoimmunity.
Granulation tissue vs granulomaGranulation tissue (Ch 3, 5) = capillaries + fibroblasts, the scaffold of healing. Granuloma (Ch 4) = epithelioid macrophages + lymphocyte collar, destructive. Same root, opposite meaning.
The mouth shows it firstCh 4 periodontitis as the chronic-inflammation model; Ch 5 the socket; Ch 6 oral contact allergy, SLE ulcers, chlorhexidine; Ch 7 Sjögren, oral GvHD; Ch 8 the HIV oral four.
